**C006-1** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase I, EV006-1) The district centres chart the committees above the hamlets in the held belt from 1964 and STILL WATER and NIGHT LANTERN take them (EV006-2, EV002-4) → the Front's district committees govern the held belt from the contested edge by courier, and the held belt has almost nothing left for the centres to find by 1967 (F006-4, F006-18) → the corps commanders and CORDS push the method into the contested belt, where files are built from ralliers' grudges and the PRUs raid on them (F006-15) → at Duc Thanh a raid on a feud's file kills a schoolteacher's family, Hanoi's new diplomatic front carries it to the American press, and the word Phoenix enters the American vocabulary three years early as the name of a murder programme, the success of the method in the villages it was built for having made it notorious in the ones it was not (EV006-4).

**C006-4** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase I) The selected advisers speak Vietnamese, are chosen for it and stay eighteen months, and the corps keeps that tour when every other American tour is twelve (EV006-1) → by 1968 about 15,000–20,000 of them have served, and their reports from the subsectors and battalions are the honest record of the territorial war that Abrams uses for "one war" (F006-24, F006-23) → the Army's personnel system, lobbied by that constituency, keeps the corps at eighteen-month tours through the drawdown and cuts the division advisory teams before the province and district ones → when the last Americans leave in 1973 the territorials and the districts are the best-advised part of the RVNAF and the divisions the least, so that the advisory effort's gain is concentrated in the war of the hamlets and absent from the war of 1972 and 1975, which was decided by divisions (§4.P5).

**C006-3** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase I, EV006-1) Phung Hoang builds a national file to the standard of a warrant, with fingerprints and photographs, held to its rules by the American lever and the audit → when the lever lapses in 1970 the palace moves the file into the Central Intelligence Organization and uses it to vet officials and chart the opposition (EV002-6) → for the election of 1971 the provincial copies are called in and the complete file is kept in one building, which the palace can control and the provinces cannot leak → on 30 April 1975 the destruction plan for that one building needs the order of a director who has already left, and the victors take intact the most complete list of the Republic's friends the war produced, the care that made the file accurate having made it whole, and its capture by the palace having made it capturable by the enemy (EV000-98).

**C007-2** [months] (begins in Phase II, EV007-3) The board's battalions walk their flanks and the 272nd Regiment declines the ambush on Route 13 on 4 May 1966 (F007-18) → the regiment moves its ambush to the Regional Force convoy at Bau Bang, which rides on its trucks, and kills about forty men (F007-5) → the III Corps commander, who had never asked the board for anything, asks it to take over the selection of RF company commanders, and from July 1967 the board reviews about 280 and replaces about 60 with field-commissioned lieutenants of their own provinces (EV007-4) → at Tet the district compounds of III and IV Corps are defended by RF companies under commanders the enemy's own displacement had brought under the board, so that the reform reached the territorials by the road the enemy chose for it (EV000-42).

The terminal link lands in Phase III.

**C010-1** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase I, EV010-1) The academy's manuals are printed in Vietnamese in tens of thousands and the first captured copies reach the B-2 Front's military staff in December 1964 (F010-20) → COSVN orders its local forces to study the ARVN platoon's routine, and by 1966–67 the Front's companies in the Delta attack the posts that keep the routine least and pass those that keep it (F010-19) → in the first wave of Tet at Cai Lay they take the one post whose acting leader keeps no listening post and pass the rest (EV010-4) → in August COSVN, finding the schooled posts both predictable and hard, sends the third offensive against the self-defence groups that no course reached, and 600–900 of their members die in three provinces (EV009-4). The enemy's knowledge of the army's routine sent his war to the people the routine did not protect.

**C010-2** [war-shaping] (begins in Phase II, EV010-3) The field commissions take the best-schooled sergeants first, and the squads they leave are given to corporals first class who have passed the leader's course (F010-15, EC010-3) → by 1968 the acting leader is the ordinary road to sergeant, and the leader's course is the real selection of the army's NCOs (EV000-51) → the waiting for the course becomes the enlisted men's grievance, and the palace's National Day decree of 1970 promotes 40,000–60,000 men past it for their gratitude (EV010-6) → the training command answers not by contesting the stripes but by barring the next promotion, and the gate survives the palace because the only men it still governs are the ones the corps commanders do not care about. The decree that broke the gate taught the palace that it did not need to break it.

**C010-3** [months] (begins in Phase II, EV010-2) The Bien Hoa academy fills in 1966 and the Army waives the Basic Leader Course for one in four rifle-company promotions to staff sergeant (F010-13) → the waiver is replaced by a ninety-day deferral that holds where the academy has places and becomes a second waiver where it does not → in 1969–71 the units with the heaviest turnover and the worst discipline are the ones whose staff sergeants are most often deferred, so the schooled sergeant is thinnest where the decay is worst (EV010-5) → the 23rd Division's own figures of 1970 show the platoons with deferred sergeants carrying about half again the drug cases and refusals of the others, and the inspector's report is read in Washington as evidence that the course works rather than that the war's units are failing. A peacetime rule's wartime exception decided where the rule mattered.

## Cards

# Card 006 — Phung Hoang (Phoenix) formalized and modernized from 1964; US unit rotation in place of individual replacement; a selected advisory corps on 18-month tours with 2026 training

*Memorandum 006 · status complete · full record: memos/006/ · generated by fie.py*

## P006a · Phung Hoang (Phoenix) Programme, formalized 1 January 1964 and built to 2026 practice: a national Phung Hoang Committee, Province and District Intelligence and Operations Coordinating Centres (PIOCC and DIOCC) in every province and district, an F3EAD targeting cycle with network analysis and document exploitation, SEEK II-class biometric enrolment of detainees and ralliers, warrant-based targeting under the 1964 police statute, the Provincial Reconnaissance Units raised under that statute, capture-first rules, no quotas, and an independent audit of neutralization claims
One national programme [U]: a national committee and centre, 44 PIOCCs and about 240 DIOCCs at full coverage [E: the period's province and district count], of which about 20 PIOCCs and 100 DIOCCs by end 1964 and all by end 1965 [E: the security-limited occupation of P002a's posts]; about 4,000–5,000 Vietnamese staff in the centres [E: 10–15 per DIOCC, 25–40 per PIOCC, about 150 nationally]; about 1,500 biometric kits [E: one per district station and centre plus field teams] · spaces ~600 US personnel, of whom ~450 military spaces [E: one or two advisers per DIOCC in contested districts, three per PIOCC, a national cell of about 60, an exploitation and analysis detachment of about 80, about 40 biometrics contractors] · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIND, FIX, SUBVERT, SECURE, ADVISE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical Phoenix: ICEX mid-1967, Phung Hoang decree December 1967, ended December 1972; 81,740 neutralized 1968–72, 26,369 killed, about 87% of the killed from conventional operations [M006·S1]
- Centres: national centre ~150 staff, 44 PIOCCs of 25–40, ~240 DIOCCs of 10–15; ~4,000–5,000 Vietnamese staff [E: historical DIOCC manning]
- Build-up: ~100 DIOCCs and 20 PIOCCs by end 1964, all by end 1965 [E: P002a's post occupation]
- PRUs under the police statute from 1964: ~44 units, ~3,000–4,500 men by 1966 [E: historical PRU of ~4,000–5,000 by 1969]
- Throughput: ~2,400–4,800 developed targets a month at full coverage; 30–50% of warrants executed within a month in the held belt, under 10% in the contested belt [E: D5]
- Biometrics: ~1,500 SEEK II kits, offline watchlist up to 120,000 [M006·S3]
- US personnel: ~600, of whom ~450 military spaces [E: D2]
- Cost: ~$15–25 million a year [E: 1964 prices]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not find the main force.** It targets the infrastructure inside the population; it does nothing against a PAVN or VC regiment (A6).
- **It does not work without night security.** In the contested belt it names cadres from ralliers and prisoners and can only raid; raids on thin files kill the wrong men.
- **It is not the 2026 targeting machine.** It keeps the method and loses its inputs: no telephones to exploit, no drones over the hamlet, no data network. The biometric kits work offline against a watchlist of up to 120,000.
- **It is not a new police.** It is a coordinating layer and a method over P002a's Special Branch; without that branch it has nothing to coordinate.
- **It does not make the army share.** The decree puts the army and the Military Security Service in the room; it does not make them hand over their best files.
- **It does not stop the infrastructure regenerating.** Cadres lost in the South are replaced from the North and the sanctuaries; arrest rate is not the measure, replacement rate is.
- **It does not protect itself from capture.** A national file on every suspected cadre is the most valuable instrument a President can seize against his opposition.

**Denies the enemy.** Where night security holds, it denies the infrastructure its upper layer: the district and province committee members whom the hamlet police seldom reach, named from ralliers, prisoners and documents and arrested on warrant from 1965 rather than 1968. It denies the cadre arrested twice under two names his second identity. It denies the Front the propaganda of the historical Phoenix wherever the rules hold. It denies nothing in the villages the Front holds and nothing against the main force.

**Verdict.** In this war Phung Hoang is a coordinating layer and a method placed over a Special Branch that already exists, and its value is the difference between a police that knows the hamlet and one that knows the district committee above it. Where the police posts and the Popular Forces hold at night, it should roughly double the share of senior cadres among those neutralized and do it four years earlier than history, with fewer false arrests, because it has no quotas and its files are built to warrant. Where night security is absent it becomes the historical Phoenix, and its 2026 label will not change that. Its greatest risks are penetration of a fused centre, the press and Congress, and capture by the palace after the Americans leave. It is a real addition to the war against the infrastructure and none at all to the war against the main force.

**Pushes:** FIND.vci +1, VCI.strength -1, SUBVERT.defection +1, POP.civilian_harm -1, US.credibility_gap +1, US.personnel_demand +1 · **Depends on:** GVN.police, POP.night_control, INTEL.penetration, GVN.political_stability, GVN.corruption, GVN.admin_capacity, ADVISE.leverage, SUBVERT.defection, US.political_tolerance

## P006b · US unit rotation for Southeast Asia: Army and Marine Corps battalions and brigades manned together, stabilised, trained collectively and deployed as units for 12-month tours in place of the individual replacement system, with commanders serving the unit's whole tour, relief in place by whole units with an overlap, battle-loss replacement in trained packets, and the 2026 Army's unit-manning and pre-deployment collective training practice
Applied to every US Army and Marine Corps maneuver battalion and its supporting brigade units deployed to the Republic from 1965 [U]: about 30 battalions in 1965 rising to about 105–110 at the 1968–69 peak [E: the historical deployment of Army and Marine maneuver battalions]; combat support and service units rotate by company and detachment [E: the scale at which they are organised] · spaces ~3–5% above the historical in-country strength on average [E: relief in place with a two- to three-week overlap, about 6% of the year, for each unit once a year]; no new spaces otherwise, and the rotation base in the United States is outside the ceiling · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical: individual 12-month (Army) and 13-month (Marine) tours; six-month command tours from 1965; no reserve mobilization [M006·S4] [M006·S5]
- Battalions: ~30 maneuver battalions in 1965, ~105–110 at the 1968–69 peak [E: historical deployment]
- Reliefs: ~105–110 a year at the peak, ~2 a week; 2–3 week overlap [E: 2026 practice]
- Extra spaces: ~3–5% average in theater, ~15,000–25,000 at the peak [E: overlap arithmetic]
- Rotation base: ~2 battalions in the cycle at home for each deployed [D]
- Unit cycle: ~4 months individual training, 6–7 months unit training, 12 months deployed within a 24-month draft term [D]
- Losses: 30–50% of riflemen in the heaviest-engaged battalions over a year, refilled by packets of 4–10 [E: period casualty rates]
- 2026 comparison: 9-month BCT tours from 2012, goal of 24 months at home [M006·S6]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not change the tour.** Each man still serves 12 months, and the total number of soldiers needed is about the same [D].
- **It does not keep local knowledge.** A whole battalion arrives new to its area once a year, and a relief in place passes perhaps half of what the outgoing unit knew.
- **It does not survive heavy losses.** A battalion that loses half its riflemen is refilled until it is again a unit of strangers.
- **It does not make bad leaders good.** It keeps commanders for the whole tour, good and bad.
- **It does not stop the late-war breakdown of discipline.** That followed the war's politics and the draft more than the replacement system.
- **It does not fit the draft term easily.** A battalion must deploy within about seven months of forming or its draftees leave before the tour ends.
- **It does not touch the ARVN.** It is an American personnel policy.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the American unit of strangers with a new commander every six months: the platoon that does not know its own men, the company that forgets its lessons, the ambush sprung by the newest man. It gives him back one thing: a whole battalion new to its area once a year, at a time he can predict.

**Verdict.** Unit rotation trades a constant trickle of strangers for a yearly flood of them. Inside the tour it gives the American battalion stable leaders, collective training before it deploys, and men who know each other, and that should make it fight better at night, in the ambush and under fire, and lose fewer men in its middle months. It costs a few percent more men in theater, a larger formed rotation base without the reserves, and a battalion that knows nothing of its area once a year. The best study of the war doubts that individual rotation was the cause of the late-war breakdown, and this provision will not prevent it. The gain is real and moderate: it improves American units, it does not change which battles the enemy accepts.

**Pushes:** US.unit_quality +2, US.casualties -1, US.personnel_demand +1, FIX.capability +1 · **Depends on:** US.political_tolerance, US.casualties, LOG.ports, ENEMY.engagement_control, US.personnel_demand

## P006c · Selected US Advisory Corps: field advisers to the RVNAF and the territorial forces (battalion, regiment, division, sector and subsector, and mobile advisory teams) chosen by board and assessment from volunteers, serving 18-month tours, trained to the 2026 Security Force Assistance Brigade standard (Military Advisor Training Academy course, Vietnamese language to working level, culture and rapport, foreign weapons, combat medicine, and fire-support and air-request qualification), with career protection and promotion priority
Every US field advisory post below corps [U]: about 3,500 in 1964 rising to about 8,000–9,000 in 1968–69 [E: MACV field advisory strength of the period, including the mobile advisory teams from 1967 per S9]; about 2,300 new advisers a year in 1964 and about 5,500–6,000 a year at the peak [E: posts divided by 1.5 years, plus about 10% losses] · spaces ~0 net in RVN [E: the posts exist historically; the 18-month tour fills them with fewer men a year]; outside RVN about 1,500–3,000 officers and NCOs in the pipeline at any time [E: about 32–36 weeks of language and adviser training for each year's entrants] · arrives 1964-01-01 · ADVISE, FIX, SECURE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Posts: ~3,500 field advisory posts in 1964, ~8,000–9,000 in 1968–69 [E: MACV field advisory strength]
- Annual intake: ~2,300 in 1964, ~5,500–6,000 at the peak [E: posts ÷ 1.5 + 10%]
- Training: ~32–36 weeks (6-week MATA, ~24 weeks Vietnamese, 2–4 weeks weapons, medicine, fires) against historical 2–8 weeks [E: D1] [M006·S9]
- Historical MATs: 354 authorized, more than 300 operating, five men each, from late 1967 [M006·S9]
- 2026 SFAB: ~800 in 36 teams of 12 advisers and 8 security; attrition up to 70% in the 1st SFAB [M006·S10]
- Pipeline: ~1,500–3,000 in training at any time outside RVN [E: D2]
- Volunteers needed: ~4,000–5,000 in 1964, ~10,000–12,000 a year at the peak at a 40–60% pass rate [E: D5]
- Cost: ~$25–35 million a year in 1964, ~$60–90 million at the peak [E: 1964 prices]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not add authority.** The adviser still has no command over his counterpart; longer tours and language deepen influence, not power.
- **It does not create Vietnamese leaders.** Advice changes a commander who will listen, not one who will not.
- **It does not make advisers fluent.** About 24 weeks of Vietnamese gives working conversation, not native ease [E: DLI course lengths].
- **It does not come free.** The good captains and NCOs it takes are taken from American units.
- **It does not arrive at once.** The first selected advisers reach the field in the second half of 1964; about a third are in post by the end of the first year.
- **It does not end dependence on American fire.** An adviser who can call air and artillery deepens the advised unit's reliance on it unless he is told not to.
- **It does not survive the withdrawal.** It is American and leaves with the Americans.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the adviser who cannot speak to his counterpart and leaves just as he learns, and the American report that says what the career needs rather than what the adviser saw. It denies him nothing at the regiment level and nothing once the Americans are gone.

**Verdict.** A selected advisory corps on 18-month tours, trained in language and advising to the 2026 standard, is the most direct answer this war can give to the advisory problem the record names: advisers without authority, of falling quality, who leave as they learn. It buys an adviser who is effective for about twelve months instead of six, speaks to his counterpart without an interpreter, and can report honestly. It does not buy authority, it does not make a bad commander good, and it takes good officers from American units. Its effect is a band in advisory leverage, ARVN effectiveness and the territorial forces, and a band against the credibility gap; it is lost when the Americans leave.

# Card 007 — Officer education to the 2026 standard for new US and ARVN officers from 1957, gating promotion; ARVN officer selection and promotion reform

*Memorandum 007 · status complete · full record: memos/007/ · generated by fie.py*

## P007a · US officer education to the 2026 standard for new officers of the Army and Marine Corps (and the Air Force and Navy continua), commissioned from 1957: the Army's Basic Officer Leader Course (BOLC A and B), Captains Career Course with its distributed-learning phase, and Command and General Staff Officer Course (Intermediate Level Education); the Marine Corps' Basic School, Expeditionary Warfare School and Command and Staff College; each course a gate for the next promotion
Every new US officer commissioned from 1957 [U]: about 15,000–20,000 Army and Marine officers a year in 1957–64, rising to about 40,000–50,000 a year at the 1967–69 peak [E: active Army and Marine officer accessions of the period, with the wartime OCS expansion]; the 1957–63 classes completed it before the campaign opened [U: standing condition officer_cohorts_1957] · spaces ~0 in RVN [E: every course is taught in the United States]; about 1,500–2,500 instructor and staff spaces added to the training base in the United States by 1967, outside the ceiling [E: student load at 2026 small-group ratios]; in effect about 4–6% of the company- and field-grade officer strength in school at any time instead of in units [E: course lengths against career length]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · ADVISE, FIX, SECURE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Courses: Army BOLC B (branch, ~4–6 months, separation if not done within 2 years of commissioning) [M007·S6]; Captains Career Course with a 75-hour distributed phase [M007·S12]; CGSOC 10 months resident [M007·S8]; USMC TBS ~6 months [E: commonly given], EWS 41 weeks [M007·S10]
- Gates: BOLC B before 1LT, CCC or EWS before MAJ, staff course before LTC [E: 2026 sequence applied as a hard bar per the grant]
- Accessions: ~15,000–20,000 Army and Marine officers a year in 1957–64, ~40,000–50,000 a year at the 1967–69 peak [E: period accessions]
- 1957–63 classes: ~100,000–130,000 commissioned, about two-thirds still serving in 1964 [E: accessions less obligated-service losses]
- First educated battalion commanders: about 1971–72 [E: promotion timing]
- Cost: ~4–6% of company- and field-grade officers in school at any time; ~1,500–2,500 added instructors at the peak; 0 spaces in RVN [E: D2, D8]
- Margin: an educated platoon leader is about as competent in month one as a historical one in months four to six [X-007]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not reach the men who run the war.** Battalion, brigade and division commanders and every general in 1964–70 were commissioned before 1957 and are untouched; the first educated battalion commanders arrive about 1971–72.
- **It is not a counterinsurgency course.** The 2026 curriculum is built first for large-scale combat against a peer; the Iraq and Afghanistan lessons are present but secondary.
- **It does not change the strategy, the body count or the replacement system.** It makes better junior officers inside them; P006b's unit rotation, not this, addresses the replacement system.
- **It does not raise commissioning standards.** It educates officers after they are commissioned; it does not impose the 2026 degree requirement on Officer Candidate School.
- **It costs captains.** At any time about one captain in eight is in school from 1966, and the wartime pipeline for platoon leaders is three to four months longer.
- **It does not teach the hamlet.** Its knowledge of Vietnam comes from Americans who served there, not from the Vietnamese.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy some of the young American officer's mistakes: the platoon walked into a horseshoe ambush on a trail, the company that loses its fire support plan in the first minutes of contact, the lieutenant who cannot read the map in the canopy. It denies him nothing at the operational level.

**Verdict.** This is a modest provision for the American side of the war and a real one. It makes the platoon leaders and company commanders of 1964–70 markedly better at their work, which saves American lives at the margin and some Vietnamese civilian lives where the lieutenant's discipline over fire and detainees holds. It does not touch the men who decide how the war is fought until the war is nearly over, and it is built for a different war from the one of 1964–65. Its largest value may be indirect: as the faculty and the common language for its ARVN counterpart, and as the education of the advisers who remain when the American units leave.

**Pushes:** US.unit_quality +1, US.casualties -1, POP.civilian_harm -1, US.personnel_demand +1 · **Depends on:** US.political_tolerance, US.unit_quality, US.personnel_demand

## P007b · RVNAF officer education to the 2026 standard for new ARVN officers commissioned from 1957: a branch basic course after commissioning at Thu Duc or Dalat, a Captains Career Course and a resident Command and General Staff course at Dalat built on the US 2026 curricula in Vietnamese, with MAAG and MACV faculty advisers, each course a gate for the next promotion
Every new ARVN officer commissioned from 1957 [U]: about 2,000–3,000 a year in 1957–63, about 4,000–6,000 a year in 1964–67 and about 8,000–12,000 a year at the 1968–71 peak [E: Thu Duc's 40,900 graduates 1952–Nov 1969 per S2, Dalat's fewer than 200 a year per S3, and the mobilization of 1968]; seven classes of about 13,000–18,000 officers completed the basic course before 1964 [E: same basis; U: standing condition officer_cohorts_1957] · spaces ~350–500 US personnel in RVN, of whom ~300–450 military spaces [E: faculty advisers and translators at three schools and a curriculum cell at the JGS Central Training Command, against the historical school advisory detachments]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · ADVISE, FIX, SECURE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical sources of officers: Thu Duc, over 40,900 graduates 1952–Nov 1969 [M007·S2]; Dalat under 200 a year before 1967 [M007·S3]; candidate course cut 37 to 24 weeks in June 1968 [M007·S2]
- Historical schooling: field-grade command and staff schools only from 1967; ninth-grade diploma required for major; most officers without formal training in 1969 [M007·S1]
- Commissions under the provision: ~2,000–3,000 a year in 1957–63, ~4,000–6,000 in 1964–67, ~8,000–12,000 at the 1968–71 peak [E: S2 and S3 averages and the mobilization]
- 1957–63 classes: ~13,000–18,000 commissioned, ~10,000–14,000 serving on 1 Jan 1964 [E: same]
- Gates: branch basic course (~4–5 months) before 1LT, career course (~5–6 months) before MAJ, Dalat staff course (~9–10 months) before LTC [U] [E: US models]
- US spaces: ~300–450 military of ~350–500 US personnel [E: faculty advisers]; Vietnamese instructors ~600–1,800 added [E: 2026 ratios]
- Battalion commanders with full education: ~1 in 5 historically, ~4 in 5 by 1967 [X-007]
- Officers in school at any time: ~5–8% of company- and field-grade [E: course lengths]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not reach the generals.** Corps and division commanders and the juntas of 1964–70 were commissioned before 1957; command at the top stays a political appointment until P007c reaches it.
- **It does not choose commanders.** It makes officers eligible; it does not put them in command. Without P007c the educated captain can be passed over for a loyalist.
- **It does not pay officers.** An educated captain whose salary has lost its value to inflation is as corruptible as an uneducated one.
- **It does not teach night security by itself.** The territorial war is learned by living in it; the course gives the vocabulary, not the trust of a hamlet.
- **It costs majors.** The career-course gate slows the making of majors in the grade the army was shortest of; only the 1957–63 classes, already through it, cover the gap in 1964–67.
- **It does not keep officers out of politics.** An educated officer corps with blocked promotion is a coup faction.
- **It deepens the habit of American fire support.** Common doctrine makes combined operations easier and the dependence on American fire deeper.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the ARVN battalion that walks down the road into the ambush the regiment laid for it: the incompetent company commander, the fire plan never made, the relief column that does not scout its route. It denies him some of the ARVN's tactical predictability, which the enemy's regiments exploited from Binh Gia onwards. It does not deny him the political general who orders the battalion to stand still.

**Verdict.** This is a substantial provision. With the 1957–63 classes in place, the ARVN's company-grade officers in 1964 are educated to a standard the historical army never reached, and from 1965 the battalions are commanded by them. That attacks the ARVN's most cited weakness — poor leadership, which American advisers named as the foremost reason for ineffective units — from below, and it does so in the years the war was lost in the countryside. Its ceiling is set above it: education does not choose commanders, pay officers or govern the generals. It makes P007c possible, because a merit system needs a pool of qualified officers to choose from, and it enlarges the small pool of able field-grade officers the record says every reform drew on. Alone it is a +1 to ARVN effectiveness; with a selection system that uses it, much more.

**Pushes:** ARVN.leadership +2, ARVN.effectiveness +1, ARVN.self_sufficiency +1, RFPF.effectiveness +1, ADVISE.leverage +1 · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.political_stability, GVN.corruption

## P007c · RVNAF Officer Selection and Promotion Reform, 1964: an independent Officer Selection and Promotion Board under the Joint General Staff with written criteria, a two-tier rater and senior-rater evaluation report on the 2026 US model with a capped top block, centrally selected battalion and regimental command lists, relief for cause, an open path to commission for proven NCOs, removal of the diploma bar to promotion, and general-officer promotion and division command filled from a ranked board list, protected by an American aid condition
One national board system [U]: about 12,000–16,000 officer promotions and about 150–250 battalion and regimental command selections a year in 1964–67 [E: an officer corps of about 18,000–24,000 regular officers in 1964 growing toward 50,000–60,000 by 1972, with the 1969 increment of 2,653 senior officers per S1] · spaces ~60–90 US personnel, of whom ~40–60 military spaces [E: an advisory cell to the board and the JGS personnel directorate, evaluation-system trainers, and a share of the senior advisers' time]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · ADVISE, SECURE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical: Diem's President chose from a confidential list [M007·S4]; corps and division commanders appointed for loyalty [M007·S5]; ninth-grade diploma for major; 80 of 133 battalion commanders in command a year or less in May 1971; 46 of 133 battalions captain-led [M007·S1]
- Board: ~200–350 Vietnamese staff; ~40–80 senior officers on panels [E: design]
- Throughput: ~12,000–16,000 promotions and ~150–250 command selections a year in 1964–67 [E: officer corps of ~18,000–24,000 regulars in 1964]
- Command tour: fixed 18–24 months [E: design]
- OER: senior-rater top block capped at about a third [E: 2026 US model]
- General officers: President chooses from a board's ranked list of three, enforced by an aid condition [E: design]
- US personnel: ~60–90, of whom ~40–60 military [E: design]
- Margin: competent battalion commanders ~1/2 historically to ~3/4 by 1967; median command tour under 1 year to ~18 months; 1–2 division commands in 10 changed by 1967 [X-007]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not take command of divisions and corps out of politics.** The President still appoints generals, from a ranked list of three; the aid condition can enforce the list, not the choice.
- **It does not stop coups.** A coup is a promotion list written by force; the reform raises its price and raises the risk of one while it beds in.
- **It does not create able officers.** It chooses among those that exist; its pool is P007b's educated classes and the small pool of able field-grade officers the record says every reform already draws on.
- **It does not see loyalty or penetration.** The board reads performance, not a man's faction, his patrons, or his contact with the enemy.
- **It does not work without the American lever,** and the lever weakens after 1969 and is gone after 1973.
- **It does not end corruption.** It makes the sale of commands harder and visible; it does not raise pay.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the ARVN battalion led by a commander who bought his command, holds it for six months and is never relieved; and, slowly, the division led by a general chosen because he would never move against the palace. It denies the enemy part of the predictability he exploited — the commander who would not close with the enemy because his career depended on avoiding losses.

**Verdict.** This is the provision that decides whether the education is used. Below the generals it works: battalions get chosen commanders who serve full tours and are relieved when they fail, and educated officers rise. At the top it is as strong as the American will to enforce a list, and no stronger; the junta years of 1964–65 will test it at once. It is the first serious answer in this war to the gap in the officer corps that the record holds open, and it is the reform most likely to provoke the generals it threatens. I judge it worth that risk. Its effect is institutional and accrues over years: it will show in battalion outcomes from 1966 and in the divisions only if the lever holds.

# Card 008 — A South Vietnamese industrial base one generation above 1964, standing from 1 January 1964: metallurgy and machining; electronics manufacturing

*Memorandum 008 · status complete · full record: memos/008/ · generated by fie.py*

## P008a · Republic of Vietnam metallurgical and machining industrial base, one generation above the RVN's actual 1964 state, standing on 1 January 1964: an electric-arc-furnace steelworks with billet casting and bar, rod, light-section and light-plate rolling at Bien Hoa; a special-steel melt, forge and heat-treatment shop; a national arsenal for small-arms components, cartridge cases and projectile bodies; engine, vehicle and weapons rebuild works; a steel boatyard; structural fabrication for bridges and fortifications; and agricultural machinery shops, with their workforce, engineers and capital
One national industrial base [U: one generation leap, South Vietnam only, standing from 1 Jan 1964]: about 200,000–300,000 t/yr of electric-arc crude steel, about 35,000–50,000 Vietnamese workers and about 1,200–1,800 engineers [E: a mini-mill and arsenal complex at the scale South Korea built 1971–76 per S3 and S4, scaled to a country of about 16 million] · spaces ~0 US military spaces [E: no uniformed staff; ordnance and engineer advisers already in the advisory structure]; about 150–300 American, Japanese and European contract engineers and licensor technicians, civilian and outside the ceiling [E: licensor teams of the period]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · SUSTAIN, SECURE, ADVISE · infrastructure

**Key figures.**
- Electric-arc crude steel about 200,000–300,000 t/yr at full rate from about 1966; about 100,000–150,000 t/yr in 1964–65 for want of scrap [E: two 30-t furnaces; scrap availability]
- Construction and fortification steel 120,000–180,000 t/yr; fabricated bridge steel 8,000–15,000 t/yr, 150–300 short spans a year [E: D3, a scrap mini-mill and fabrication works]
- Cartridge cases and bullets 150–250 million 5.56 and 7.62mm a year; 105mm bodies 400,000–600,000 and mortar bodies 1–1.5 million a year — all filled with imported propellant and explosive [E: D3, two forging lines and four case-and-bullet lines]
- Engine rebuild 3,000–5,000 and transmission rebuild 1,500–2,500 a year; 400–600 M113s and M41s rebuilt a year [E: D3, a rebuild works of 4,000–6,000 men]
- Workforce 35,000–50,000 with 1,200–1,800 engineers; 25,000–35,000 men of military age needing deferment [E: D1–D2, Korean ratios scaled]
- Electricity 70–100 MW at peak; Da Nhim's line plus a 66 MW Thu Duc thermal station [E: D5, melt-shop power demand]
- Imports by value about 40–60% of output; by weight a quarter to a third [E: D8, an EAF mill and arsenal import bill]
- Stretches each ammunition and parts aid dollar about 1.4–1.8 times [E: this memorandum's design of the base]
- RVN industry in 1964 about a tenth of output, with 85% of firms in Saigon, Bien Hoa and Gia Dinh [M008·S1]

**Negative specification.** This base makes metal, not war materiel. It cannot make propellant, high explosive or primers. Every cartridge, shell and mine it produces is filled with imported chemicals, so it stretches the ammunition supply but cannot replace it. It makes no fuel or lubricants, no aircraft, no engines larger than small diesels, no artillery tubes beyond rebuild, no tanks and no armour plate beyond light plate. It does not make the 2026 M4A1 upper receiver of P004a to its original tolerance, only magazines, springs, small parts and, after its barrel line is proven, chrome-lined barrels. It does not find, fix or kill anyone, and it touches neither half of the find-and-fix problem. It does not secure a single hamlet: it makes the wire, and the wire is worth what the Popular Forces behind it are worth. It is only useful if the RVNAF orders from it, and in a war where the American article is free, it will not do so unless made to. It depends on imported electrodes, alloys and machine-tool spares paid in aid dollars, and on power lines that run through contested country.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the Front the long repair times of a country that waits on ships: blown bridges, cut rail and wrecked outposts come back in weeks instead of months. After 1973 it denies Hanoi part of the bet that an American aid cut would starve the RVNAF of parts and ammunition. It does not deny him sanctuary, infiltration or initiative, and its own scrap, wire and brass are a new source for his workshops through the black market.

**Verdict.** This is a slow provision, and its weight falls late. In 1964–67 it builds bridges and outposts faster, keeps more trucks and carriers running, and gives the farmer a pump. All of that is useful and none of it changes a battle. From 1968 it shortens the RVNAF's repair cycle and puts its construction and bridging on its own feet. In 1973–75 it may matter a great deal, because it stretches every aid dollar for ammunition and parts by something like half again, at exactly the moment the dollars run short. It will do that only if American policy forces the RVNAF to buy from it during the years when American supply is free. Otherwise the arsenal starves and is a shell when it is needed. It is a real step toward an RVNAF that can supply itself. It is not self-sufficiency, because propellant, explosive, fuel and every major weapon still come from abroad.

## P008b · Republic of Vietnam electronics manufacturing base, one generation above the RVN's actual 1964 state, standing on 1 January 1964: a communications plant for licensed VHF-FM manpack and vehicle radios (AN/PRC-10, then AN/PRC-25 and AN/PRC-77 class) and hamlet and village radios; a dry-cell and storage-battery works; a wire and cable mill including WD-1/TT field wire; passive-component, transformer and printed-circuit shops; a foreign-owned discrete-transistor assembly and test plant; consumer radio assembly; and a signal and electronics rebuild depot, with their workforce, engineers and capital
One national electronics base [U: one generation leap, South Vietnam only, standing from 1 Jan 1964]: about 15,000–25,000 military manpack and vehicle radios, 20,000–30,000 hamlet and village radios, 1.5–3 million radio dry cells and 60,000–100,000 km of field wire a year at full rate, about 20,000–35,000 workers and 600–1,000 engineers [E: South Korea's electronics sector of about 1971–74 per S5, scaled] · spaces ~0 US military spaces [E: signal advisers already in the advisory structure]; about 100–200 contract engineers and licensor technicians, civilian and outside the ceiling [E: licensor teams of the period]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · SUSTAIN, SECURE, STRIKE, ADVISE · infrastructure

**Key figures.**
- Military manpacks and vehicle sets 15,000–25,000 a year at full rate: PRC-10 in 1964–65, PRC-25 from about 1966, PRC-77 from about 1969 [E: licence the year after US fielding, S6, S7]
- Village and hamlet radios 20,000–30,000 a year [E: this memorandum's design of the base]
- Radio dry cells 1.5–3 million a year; a PRC-25 battery lasts 2–3 hours heavy use, several days light [E: D3, a Korean-scale battery works; battery life per S7] [M008·S7]
- Field wire 60,000–100,000 km a year [E: this memorandum's design of the base]
- Radio rebuilds 30,000–50,000 a year, plus AN/PPS-5 module and avionics bench repair [E: D3, a depot of 2,500–3,500]
- Workforce 20,000–35,000, mostly women on assembly; 600–1,000 engineers; 6,000–10,000 men of military age in technician grades [E: D1–D2, Korean assembly-industry ratios scaled]
- Imported content about half of output by value; semiconductors and crystals all imported [E: D8, assembly-industry practice]
- Stretches the aid dollar for communications about two times; nearly ends the 1974–75 battery shortage [E: D9, the share of value added in country]
- Korea's electronics exports $3.6 million in 1966, target $100 million by 1971 [M008·S5]

**Negative specification.** This base assembles and repairs; it does not invent or fabricate chips. It makes no semiconductor dice and no quartz crystals in volume, so every radio depends on imports. It builds only American-licensed sets, each about a year after the US Army fields it: PRC-10s in 1964–65, PRC-25s from about 1966, PRC-77s from about 1969. It does not build encryption (NESTOR and all COMSEC equipment stay American-controlled), radar, avionics, sensors, satellite equipment, or anything resembling the 2026 systems of earlier provisions. It repairs radar and avionics modules; it does not make them. It does nothing about canopy, terrain or monsoon propagation. A Vietnamese-built PRC-25 has the same range as an American one. It does not find the main force or identify the VCI. It does not secure a hamlet: it lets the hamlet call for help, which is worth what the help is worth. Radios and batteries issued in contested hamlets will leak to the enemy.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the Front the silent outpost. A Popular Forces post that can call the district, the artillery and the reaction force at night is harder to overrun and its defenders are harder to frighten into leaving. After 1973 it denies Hanoi the RVNAF's communications collapse that a battery and parts famine would bring. It gives the Front more captured radios and batteries than before.

**Verdict.** Of the two provisions this is the more important, and it is important in a narrow, specific way. It puts a working radio and a battery in Popular Forces outposts and hamlets four or five years earlier than history did, and keeps them working with a depot and a battery works in country. The night war in the hamlets is decided by whether a squad behind wire can call for help and whether help comes, and this is the half of that equation that was missing. It also keeps the RVNAF's communications alive in 1974–75, when the real force rationed batteries. It does nothing for finding the enemy, builds no system Hanoi need fear, and depends wholly on imported semiconductors. Its value in any hamlet is set by whether the artillery and the reaction force answer the call. Where they do, I expect the territorial forces to be measurably harder to break at night. Where they do not, it is a radio that reports the hamlet's fall.

# Card 009 — Basic training to the 2026 standard for every US and RVNAF enlisted entrant from 1957, with an abridged course for the Regional and Popular Forces

*Memorandum 009 · status complete · full record: memos/009/ · generated by fie.py*

## P009a · US entry-level training to the 2026 standard for every enlisted entrant from 1957: the Army's 10-week Basic Combat Training (Yellow, Red, White and Blue phases, the Hammer, the Anvil and the Forge field exercises, Forge 2.5 collective-event design, the 2018 discipline and first-aid redesign), the Marine Corps' 13-week recruit training with the Crucible, the Navy's 10-week recruit training and the Air Force's 7.5-week Basic Military Training, each with its 2026 tactical combat casualty care and fitness content; basic training only, no advanced individual training, OSUT, School of Infantry or Marine Combat Training
Every US enlisted entrant from 1957 [U]: about 450,000–550,000 a year in 1957–64 and about 800,000–1,000,000 a year at the 1966–68 peak across the four services [E: Selective Service inductions of 82,060–142,246 a year in 1957–64 and 382,010 in 1966 per S8, with volunteers two to three times the inductees]; the 1957–63 entrants completed it before the campaign opened [U: standing condition enlisted_bct_1957] · spaces ~0 in RVN [E: every course is taught in the United States]; about 3,000–5,000 added drill sergeants, drill instructors and support cadre in the United States at the 1966–68 peak, and about 20,000–25,000 more trainee man-years in the Army pipeline at any time from the two added weeks, all outside the ceiling [E: D2]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Courses: Army BCT 10 weeks in four phases with the Hammer, the Anvil and the Forge [M009·S1]; Marine recruit training 13 weeks, Navy 10, Air Force BMT 7.5 [M009·S4]
- Historical Army basic course: 8 weeks, in some cases 9 [M009·S7]
- Forge: 81 hours as a graduation requirement from 2018 [M009·S3], a four-day patrol base in Forge 2.5 from 2024 [M009·S2]
- Accessions: about 450,000–550,000 enlisted a year in 1957–64 and 800,000–1,000,000 in 1966–68, all services [E: inductions per M009·S8 with volunteers]
- 1957–63 entrants still serving on 1 Jan 1964: about 1.1–1.4 million, the junior NCOs of 1964–66 [E: D1]
- Cost: about 3,000–5,000 added drill sergeants and instructors at the peak; 20,000–25,000 more Army trainees in the pipeline at any time; build-up slowed about 2–3 months [E: D2, D5]
- Extremity hemorrhage: 7.9% of US killed in action in Vietnam, the leading preventable cause of death [M009·S14]
- Lives saved by the tourniquet reflex: about 900–1,900 Americans over 1965–72 [X-009]
- Completion: about 90% in 2026 [M009·S1]; 82–88% against the Project 100,000 intake [E: D5]

**Negative specification.** - **It is basic training only.** It does not touch advanced individual training, infantry school, NCO education or unit training; the rifleman's trade beyond the individual soldier's skills is historical.
- **It teaches nothing about Vietnam.** No booby traps, villages, paddies or Viet Cong; its scenarios are large-scale combat against a peer.
- **It does not issue a tourniquet.** It teaches the drill; the 2026 CAT does not exist, and an improvised or period tourniquet is less reliable.
- **It does not change who is drafted.** Project 100,000 and the entrance standards are untouched; the course fails more of the weak intake rather than improving it.
- **It costs sergeants and time.** About 3,000–5,000 more drill sergeants at the peak, and two more weeks for each Army recruit, which slows the 1965–66 build-up by two to three months.
- **It does not reach the senior NCOs.** Platoon sergeants and first sergeants of 1964–68 entered before 1957.
- **It decays without refreshment.** Marksmanship and casualty care are perishable; the grant gives no further training to keep them.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the wounded American who bleeds to death from a leg wound in the ten minutes before the medic reaches him, and some of the new soldier's fatal mistakes: the man who cannot hit what he aims at, who bunches up, who talks in the ambush position. It denies him nothing at the operational level.

**Verdict.** This is a modest provision for the American war with one real saving inside it. The ten-week course makes the American private and the young sergeant of 1964–68 somewhat better at the individual soldier's work, and much better for the cook and the truck driver whose basic course was all the combat training they had. Its largest single effect is the tourniquet: every American taught to stop an extremity bleed, in a war where that was the leading preventable cause of death. I estimate that at about 900–1,900 American lives over the war, which I sign for gladly. It does not change how the war is fought, it teaches nothing about the hamlet, and it costs drill sergeants and two weeks of each soldier's time during the build-up.

**Pushes:** US.unit_quality +1, MED.survival +1, US.casualties -1, US.personnel_demand +1 · **Depends on:** US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance, LOG.helicopter_hours

Every RVNAF regular enlisted entrant from 1957 [U]: about 30,000–45,000 a year in 1957–63, about 60,000–100,000 a year in 1964–67 and about 130,000–170,000 a year at the 1968–69 peak [E: Quang Trung's 24,000 a year in the mid-1950s and the 1964 plan for 30,000 per S13, and 168,335 Army and RF recruits through the training centres in 1968 per S9, less the RF share]; the 1957–63 entrants completed it before the campaign opened [U: standing condition enlisted_bct_1957] · spaces ~250–400 US personnel in RVN, of whom ~220–360 military spaces [E: advisory detachments of six to twelve at each of about 15–25 national and division training centres, a drill-sergeant academy team and a curriculum cell at the Central Training Command]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, ADVISE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Historical ARVN basic course: 8 weeks in the mid-1950s [M009·S13]; 12 weeks cut to 9 in 1968 [M009·S9]; RF 9 weeks in 1964 matching the ARVN centres [M009·S10]
- Historical untrained draftees sent straight to units [M009·S9]
- Centres: 33 in 1968–70, normal capacity about 65,000, emergency about 105,655 [M009·S9]; Quang Trung 24,000 a year in the mid-1950s, 30,000 planned in 1964 [M009·S13]
- Intake: about 30,000–45,000 regulars a year in 1957–63, 60,000–100,000 in 1964–67, 130,000–170,000 at the 1968–69 peak [E: D1]
- 1957–63 entrants still serving on 1 Jan 1964: about 120,000–160,000, half to two-thirds of the regular enlisted ranks [E: D1]
- Cadre: about 1,000–3,000 Vietnamese drill sergeants; 220–360 US military spaces in RVN [E: D2]
- Margin: the 2026-trained recruit is about as competent on his first day as a historical one after 4–6 months in a battalion [X-009]
- RVNAF lives saved by the tourniquet reflex: about 4,000–12,000 over 1964–75 [X-009]

**Negative specification.** - **It is basic training only.** It does not train the battalion, the squad leader or the specialist; unit training, which historically was "virtually nonexistent", is untouched.
- **It is not longer than history.** Ten weeks against a historical nine to twelve; the gain is in method, cadre, the weapon and the rule that nobody skips it.
- **It does not cure desertion.** Pay, family and posting far from home drove desertion, and the course touches none of them.
- **It does not choose the officer.** A trained private under a political commander is still sent down the road into the ambush; that is memoranda 007's and 002's work.
- **It costs NCOs.** About 1,000–3,000 Vietnamese drill sergeants kept out of the battalions.
- **It teaches nothing about Vietnam.** Its scenarios are large-scale combat; the trail, the village and the mine are learned in the unit.
- **It does not issue tourniquets.** It teaches the drill.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the ARVN private who cannot hit what he shoots at, who joins his battalion untrained, and who bleeds to death from a leg wound. It denies him some of the ease with which his ambushes broke ARVN units whose men had never been taught to move under fire. It denies him nothing at the operational level.

**Verdict.** This is a real provision for the ARVN, larger than P009a is for the Americans, because the gap it closes is wider. Its best effects are three: every regular soldier trained before he joins a unit, the 2026 marksmanship course on the carbine he will carry, and every Vietnamese soldier taught to stop a bleed. Its cost is the NCOs who teach it. It does not touch the officer who leads the soldier, the desertion that takes him away, or the battalion training that would make a unit of him. A better private in an army with a bad colonel is still in an army with a bad colonel, and memoranda 007 and 002 are what change the colonel.

**Pushes:** ARVN.effectiveness +1, MED.survival +1, ARVN.desertion -1 · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.corruption, ENEMY.engagement_control, ECON.inflation, LOG.helicopter_hours

## P009c · Abridged basic training on the 2026 US Army model for every Regional Forces and Popular Forces recruit (and every Civil Guard and Self-Defense Corps recruit from 1957): a six-week course of the 2026 Basic Combat Training's individual soldier skills in Vietnamese, without drill and ceremony, the Army-specific institutional blocks or the large-unit collective exercises, taught at the RF/PF training centres by Vietnamese drill sergeants with US advisers; basic training only, no further training
Every RF and PF recruit from 1957 [U]: about 20,000–35,000 a year in 1957–63, about 40,000–70,000 a year in 1964–67 and about 60,000–90,000 a year at the 1968–69 expansion [E: a Civil Guard and Self-Defense Corps of about 86,000 in 1959 per S10, desertion of 11,957–49,224 a year in 1962–65 per S12 that had to be replaced, and 22,483 PF recruits plus the RF share of 168,335 through the centres in 1968 per S9 and S12]; course length six weeks [U: abridged; E: length chosen in D1] · spaces ~200–350 US personnel in RVN, of whom ~180–320 military spaces [E: advisory teams of three to six at about 19–37 RF/PF training centres and a share of the drill-sergeant academy team]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · SECURE, ADVISE · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Course: six weeks abridged from the 2026 BCT [U: abridged; E: length chosen in D1]
- Historical: PF six weeks at centres in 26 provinces, 1960–64 [M009·S11]; RF nine weeks in 1964, refresher four weeks [M009·S10]; 1964 territorial training up to 60% behind programme [M009·S11]
- Centres: 37 cut to 19 under the Central Training Command [M009·S12]
- PF desertion: 11,957 (1962), 18,540 (1963), 36,608 (1964), 49,224 (1965) [M009·S12]
- Intake: about 20,000–35,000 a year in 1957–63, 40,000–70,000 in 1964–67, 60,000–90,000 in 1968–69 [E: D1]
- 1957–63 recruits still serving on 1 Jan 1964: about 60,000–100,000, a third to a half of the territorial forces [E: D1]
- Cadre: about 300–600 Vietnamese drill sergeants; 180–320 US military spaces in RVN [E: D2]
- Margin: the territorial recruit about as competent in the individual skills as a historical ARVN regular recruit [X-009]

**Negative specification.** - **It is not a hamlet-defence course.** It abridges the 2026 basic course; the 2026 Army has no territorial-defence course to abridge, and the grant gives no further training.
- **It is shorter than the historical RF course.** Six weeks against nine for the RF; the RF gains method and loses three weeks.
- **It does not hold the hamlet.** A trained platoon without artillery, a reaction force or a leader still loses its fort at night.
- **It does not recruit.** The district chief's control of recruiting and release is untouched.
- **It does not pay the territorial soldier.** RF/PF pay and the PF's family's safety drive desertion as before.
- **It does not touch the leader.** The PF platoon leader and the RF company commander are what the 1964 leadership training, which historically never filled its quotas, made them.
- **It does not issue tourniquets.** It teaches the drill.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the local force some of its easiest victories: the untrained PF platoon that fires all its ammunition into the dark in the first ten minutes, cannot hit the sapper at the wire, and bleeds out its wounded before dawn. It denies the VCI nothing by itself; it makes the hamlet slightly harder to enter at night.

**Verdict.** This is a modest provision on paper and a meaningful one in the hamlets. Six weeks of the 2026 course is not much training, and it is not more training than the territorial forces historically had. Its value is that every territorial soldier gets it, on the carbine memorandum 004 gave him, with the casualty drill and the conduct block that matter most to a soldier who fights among his neighbours with no helicopter coming. The territorial forces took the heaviest losses in this war and were credited with a large share of the fighting; a better-trained militia in the hamlet is the cheapest improvement in night security I can buy. It does not hold the hamlet by itself, and it does not touch the platoon leader.

**Pushes:** RFPF.effectiveness +1, POP.civilian_harm -1 · **Depends on:** RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, GVN.admin_capacity, ECON.inflation

## Employment concepts
EC009-1 the ten-week cycle at Quang Trung · EC009-2 the territorial cycle at the province centre (platoon intake) · EC009-3 the first minute and the long night (casualty care) · EC009-4 the drill sergeant's circle (with P007c) · EC009-5 the course number on the muster roll (with P001b). Abandoned: EC009-6 the course in the village (no ranges, watched by the enemy, teams ambushed) · EC009-7 the surge course (the Forge is what the new soldier most needed) · EC009-8 the American drill sergeant (obedience to a foreigner, cadre lose face, propaganda)

## Interactions
- P009b × P004a, P004c: the recruit qualifies on the carbine and squad gun he will carry, under a programme written for them; IRON GATE's five-day zeroing course becomes a refresher for men already trained, and the battalion's squad gun has a gunner who learned the gun in basic (F009-1)
- P009b × P007b, P007c: the trained private under an educated lieutenant; the drill the officer orders is the drill the private learned, and the board's field commission draws its strongest candidates from returning drill sergeants (F009-1, F009-4)
- P009c × P004a, P008b, P002b: the post's first ten minutes: a trained Popular Forces platoon with a carbine it can shoot, a radio it knows how to report on, and a chief who keeps it in the hamlet at night (F009-2)
- P009b, P009c × P001b: the course number on the muster roll; the Muster Service is the enforcement arm of the rule that nobody joins a unit untrained (F009-3)
- P009a × P006b: the trained recruit joins a battalion that trains collectively for six to seven months before it deploys; the Forge's collective events are the first rung of that training, and the battalion's training starts higher
- P009a, P009b, P009c × P006c: the selected adviser, trained in combat medicine, advises units whose soldiers already know the tourniquet; the mobile advisory teams are freed from teaching the territorials basic skills (F009-14)
- P009b, P009c × P008a: the national ranges fire about 30–80 million rounds of 5.56mm a year, the first steady domestic customer for the arsenal's cartridge-case line and a reason for the domestic share that is not a war emergency

# Card 010 — NCO education to the 2026 US standard for every US NCO and every RVNAF regular and territorial NCO from 1957, each course a gate for the next promotion

*Memorandum 010 · status complete · full record: memos/010/ · generated by fie.py*

## P010a · US enlisted professional military education to the 2026 standard for every NCO of the four services from 1957: the Army's NCO Professional Development System (the 29-day Basic Leader Course, the Advanced and Senior Leader Courses, the Master Leader Course and the 10-month Sergeants Major Course) under Select, Train, Educate, Promote; the Marine Corps' Corporals Course, Sergeants School, Career and Advanced School programmes, SNCO Leadership School and First Sergeants School; the Navy and Air Force enlisted leadership continua; each course a gate for the next promotion
Every US NCO from 1957 [U]: the NCOs serving in 1957 put through the course for their grade in 1957–60 and every man promoted since through his course before promotion; about 120,000–180,000 Army and Marine course completions a year in 1957–64 and about 250,000–350,000 at the 1967–69 peak, with about as many again in the Navy and Air Force [E: D1 and D5, from NCO strengths of the period and promotion rates]; by 1 Jan 1964 every serving NCO holds the course for his grade [U: standing condition nco_education_1957] · spaces ~250–450 US personnel in RVN [E: a MACV NCO academy at about 150–250 cadre teaching the Basic Leader Course in theater to men promoted there, and NCO course cells at the field force and Marine amphibious force headquarters]; about 4,000–7,000 added instructor and staff spaces in the United States at the peak and about 2–3% of the NCO corps in school at any time, outside the ceiling [E: D2]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Army 2026 courses: Basic Leader Course 29 days with 8 days in the field [M010·S2]; Advanced and Senior Leader Courses three weeks resident [M010·S4]; Master Leader Course three weeks [M010·S4]; Sergeants Major Course 10 months [M010·S4]
- Gates: STEP from 2016, each course for the next grade [M010·S1]; BLC the prerequisite for staff sergeant from 2025 [M010·S4]
- Waivers in peacetime: about 14,000 Army NCOs promoted without required education in 2015–16 [M010·S1]
- Historical: academies under AR 350-90 from 1958, 180,000 through by 1959 [M010·S6]; NCOES only from 1971 [M010·S5]; Sergeants Major Academy 1972 [H]
- NCO Candidate Course: 12 weeks plus 9 on the job, about 33,000 graduates 1967–72 [M010·S5]
- Volume: about 120,000–180,000 Army and Marine course completions a year before the war, 250,000–350,000 at the 1967–69 peak; 330,000–400,000 catch-up places in 1957–60 [E: D1]
- Cost: about 2–3% of NCOs in school at any time; 4,000–7,000 added instructors at the peak; 250–450 spaces in RVN [E: D2]
- Margin: a BLC-educated squad leader in month one about as competent as a historical one after three or four months in the field [X-010]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not make more NCOs.** The NCO shortage of 1966–69 was a shortage of men, made by the 12-month tour, the separations of senior NCOs and the build-up without reserves; the provision educates the men promoted, and its gates slow some promotions.
- **It does not keep the sergeant in the war.** The 12-month tour still takes him home; memorandum 006's unit rotation, not this, decides whether he stays with his men.
- **It does not cure the crisis of 1969–71.** Drugs, racial violence and fragging were the conscript army's crisis; an educated sergeant handles it better and is not immune to it.
- **It is not a Vietnam course.** The 2026 curricula teach large-scale combat; the war's own lessons enter only when men back from Vietnam teach it, from about 1966–67.
- **The gate will be waived.** The Army waived it about 14,000 times in peacetime; in a shortage it will be waived again, first for the junior grades.
- **It does not teach the trades.** The 2026 Advanced and Senior Leader Courses are three weeks of leadership, not technical schooling.
- **It costs sergeants.** About 2–3% of the NCO corps is in school at any time, and 4,000–7,000 senior NCOs teach instead of lead [E: D2].
- **It does not reach the Regional and Popular Forces, or the officers.** The first is outside the grant; the second is memorandum 007's.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy some of the American squad's mistakes: the patrol that is lost in the canopy and walks into a base camp, the ambush laid without security that is itself ambushed, the squad that loses its fire control in the first minute and shoots its own flank, the casualty left to bleed while the sergeant calls for help on the wrong frequency. It denies him the leaderless American platoon after its lieutenant is hit. It denies him nothing at the operational level and nothing in the sanctuary.

**Verdict.** This is a real provision for the American Army and a modest one for the war. It makes every American sergeant better at the work he was already doing, and in a war fought by squads and platoons that saves American lives and some Vietnamese ones. Its largest value falls in 1967–71, when the historical NCO corps was thinnest and youngest, because the instant sergeant now has at least the Basic Leader Course and the platoon sergeant the Advanced. It does not make more sergeants, keep them in Vietnam past their year, or touch the strategy they fight inside. Its indirect value may be the larger: every American NCO adviser has been through the courses his Vietnamese counterpart is learning, and that is what makes P010b work.

**Pushes:** US.unit_quality +1, US.casualties -1, US.personnel_demand +1, POP.civilian_harm -1 · **Depends on:** US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance, US.personnel_demand

## P010b · RVNAF NCO education on the 2026 US Army NCO Professional Development System for every NCO of the ARVN, Airborne, Rangers, Vietnamese Marines, VNAF and VNN and of the Regional and Popular Forces (Civil Guard and Self-Defense Corps before 1964) from 1957 (RF and PF by erratum E03): a Basic Leader Course for corporals and sergeants, an Advanced Leader Course for squad and section leaders, a Senior Leader Course for platoon sergeants, a Master Leader Course for first sergeants and battalion senior NCOs and a senior NCO course, in Vietnamese at the National NCO Academy at Nha Trang (Dong De), division and service NCO schools and the RF/PF training centres, with MAAG and MACV advisers, each course a gate for the next promotion
Every RVNAF regular and RF/PF NCO from 1957 [U]: regular NCOs about 18,000–28,000 in 1957, 35,000–50,000 in 1964 and 90,000–130,000 at the 1970 peak, RF/PF NCOs about 10,000–15,000, 25,000–40,000 and 55,000–80,000 [E: D1 and E03]; about 14,000–24,000 course completions a year in 1957–63, 27,000–45,000 in 1964–67 and 50,000–80,000 at the 1968–70 peak [E: D1 and E03, against S8's 16,522 students at the Nha Trang academy in 1970]; by 1 Jan 1964 every serving regular and territorial NCO holds the course for his grade [U: standing condition nco_education_1957] · spaces ~210–420 US personnel in RVN, of whom ~180–380 military spaces [E: an advisory detachment of 40–70 at the Nha Trang academy, teams of four to eight at 10–15 division and service NCO schools, teams of two to five at 19–37 RF/PF centres and a curriculum and translation cell at the Central Training Command; E03]; no troop ceiling is set (CONFIG) · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, ADVISE, SUSTAIN · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Courses: BLC six weeks, ALC, SLC and MLC four weeks each, senior NCO course four to five months, each a gate for the next grade [U] [E: D1, the US 2026 lengths in M010·S2 and M010·S4 lengthened for translation]
- Academy: National NCO Academy, founded 1951 as the Commando School, at Nha Trang, reorganised late 1958 for leadership [M010·S8]; 16,522 students in 1970, barracks 3,320 raised to 4,520 [M010·S8]
- Historical: leader programme of seven and ten weeks only under consideration in 1964 [M010·S9]; middle NCO grades thin, promotion by seniority, across-the-board decree promotions [M010·S11]
- Commissioning drain: over 2,000 commissioned from the ranks in 1966, including 401 regular and 100 RF master sergeants first class [M010·S10]
- NCO corps: about 18,000–28,000 in 1957, 35,000–50,000 in 1964, 90,000–130,000 at the 1970 peak [E: D1]
- Throughput: 8,000–14,000 a year in 1957–63, 15,000–25,000 in 1964–67, 30,000–45,000 at the 1968–70 peak [E: D1]
- Cost: 800–1,500 Vietnamese instructors before 1964, 2,000–3,500 at the peak; 130–270 US military spaces in RVN [E: D2]
- Margin: closes about a third to a half of the gap between an average and a good ARVN company at squad and platoon level [X-010]

**Negative specification.** - **It does not reach the Regional and Popular Forces.** Their NCOs, who led the platoons that held the hamlets, keep the schooling history gave them; the territorial war's sergeants are unchanged.
- **It does not choose the officer.** An educated sergeant under a political or incompetent commander is still sent down the road into the ambush; memoranda 007 and 002 change the commander.
- **The gate can be opened by decree.** Across-the-board promotions on national occasions were historical; a gate the government can override is a standard, not a law.
- **It costs the best sergeants.** About 800–1,500 Vietnamese instructors before 1964 and 2,000–3,500 at the peak, on top of memorandum 009's 2,000–3,000 drill sergeants.
- **It does not cure desertion.** Pay, family and posting drive it; the course touches the leader who counsels the soldier, not the pay that feeds his family.
- **It does not stop the commissioning drain.** The best senior NCOs are the best candidates for commission, and over 2,000 were commissioned in 1966 alone.
- **It teaches the technique of the after-action review, not the culture of telling the truth.** The course can teach a sergeant to report failure; it cannot make his officers want to hear it.
- **It does not reach above the company.** The battles the ARVN lost above the NCO are lost the same way.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy the ARVN platoon that sleeps in its night position without listening posts, the squad that fires all its ammunition in the first minutes and then runs, the company that loses its fire control when its officer is hit, and the patrol that takes the same path every evening. It denies him some of the ARVN's tactical predictability below the company commander, and some of the looting and abuse in the hamlets that a sergeant who controls his men prevents. It does not deny him the decision above the company.

**Verdict.** This is a substantial provision for the ARVN, larger than P010a is for the Americans, because the ARVN's NCO corps was its thinnest layer and nobody before this grant had built it. With memorandum 009's trained private and memorandum 007's educated lieutenant, the regular army from 1964 has, for the first time, a trained leader at every level from the squad to the company. That changes how ARVN small units fight at night, how they keep their weapons and trucks running, and how they treat the people in the hamlets they pass through. Its costs are the best sergeants taken to teach, in the year the army can least spare them, and a gate the government can open whenever it wishes. It does not reach the territorial forces, the commanders above the company, or the pay that keeps the soldier's family fed. A better sergeant under a bad colonel is still under a bad colonel; but in a war of squads and platoons, a better sergeant is most of what the soldier sees of the army.

**Pushes:** ARVN.effectiveness +1, ARVN.self_sufficiency +1, ARVN.desertion -1, RFPF.effectiveness +1, US.personnel_demand +1 · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.corruption, ECON.inflation, ARVN.desertion, ENEMY.engagement_control, POP.night_control, GVN.admin_capacity, STRIKE.responsiveness, ARVN.self_sufficiency

| F010-22 | Cross-boundary feedback | SUSTAIN | 300–900 US lives at 1–3% of small-unit deaths; below a band; tolerance unmoved | minor |
