## Employment concepts
EC010-1 the leader's cycle at Dong De · EC010-2 the platoon leader's course at the province centre (with P009c, P008b) · EC010-3 the acting squad leader · EC010-4 sergeant to sergeant (with P006c) · EC010-5 the academy at Bien Hoa (with P006b) · EC010-6 the returning instructor · EC010-7 the readiness report (with P008a, P001b). Abandoned: EC010-8 the course in the battalion's lull (units cancelled it) · EC010-9 the staff sergeant's waiver (one in four; replaced by priority and a 90-day deferral) · EC010-10 the American instructor at Dong De (leadership taught as American) · EC010-11 the battalion sergeant major (commanders refused an NCO channel; the sergeant's authority is what the officer allows)

## Interactions
- P010b × P009b, P009c × P007b, P007c: the trained private, the schooled sergeant and the educated lieutenant under a board-chosen commander; the chain of leadership below the company is complete, and each layer's value depends on the one above and below it (F010-1)
- P010b × P009c × P008b × P004c: the Popular Forces post at night with a trained platoon, a radio on the air, a squad gun and a platoon leader schooled to site, roster and hold it (F010-2)
- P010a, P010b × P006c: sergeant-to-sergeant advice from the same curriculum; the selected adviser's Vietnamese reaches the battalion's senior NCO who runs its training (F010-3)
- P010b × P008a, P008b: the motor and signal sergeants schooled to run maintenance and report readiness meet the rebuild depot and the battery works from the user's side (F010-4)
- P010b × P001b × P007c: the Muster Service puts each NCO's course number on the roll and the Commission pursues bought passes and decree promotions; the gate is as strong as the lever behind them (F010-5)
- P010b × P007c: the educated sergeant is the strongest candidate for the field commission; the board takes the best platoon sergeants faster, and the Basic Leader Course's acting squad leaders fill behind them (F010-15, EC010-3)
- P010a × P006b: the educated sergeant trains his squad collectively for six to seven months before the battalion deploys and keeps it for the tour; the Basic Leader Course's situational exercise becomes the squad's rehearsal
- P010a × P009a: every American drill sergeant has passed the Advanced Leader Course; the 3,000–5,000 added drill sergeants and 4,000–7,000 added NCO instructors draw on the same senior NCOs (F010-12)
- P010b × P009b: the drill sergeants who return to the battalions as platoon sergeants hold the Senior Leader Course before they take the platoon; the drill sergeant's circle runs through the academy (F010-11)


## Trajectory Log

## Memo 006 — Phung Hoang (Phoenix) formalized and modernized from 1964; US unit rotation in place of individual replacement; a selected advisory corps on 18-month tours with 2026 training

Memorandum 006 gave the Republic Phung Hoang in 1964, built behind the police posts with warrants, an audit and no quotas; it gave the American battalions unit rotation and the ARVN a selected advisory corps on eighteen-month tours. The first was the largest change: the Front's district committees in the held belt were followed out of the villages and broken in 1965–66, at Hoc Mon and Can Giuoc, three years before the historical Phoenix reached that layer, and the count was honest throughout. But success pushed the method into the contested belt, a raid at Mo Duc made "Phoenix" a scandal in 1967, and the national file, consolidated by the palace in 1971, was taken intact when Saigon fell. Unit rotation made the American battalion fight better in the contacts it was granted and gave the enemy a relief week to aim at. The advisers deepened influence and left. The end state stays at rung (a): Saigon falls on 30 April 1975.

## Memo 007 — Officer education to the 2026 standard for new US and ARVN officers from 1957, gating promotion; ARVN officer selection and promotion reform

Memorandum 007 educated every American and ARVN officer commissioned from 1957 to the 2026 standard and gave the ARVN a promotion board that chose its battalion commanders on merit, kept them eighteen months and relieved them when they failed. From 1966 the ARVN's battalions were led as the historical army's never were, and the enemy answered as he answers every better unit: he declined to fight them. The 272nd Regiment withdrew from its ambush on Route 13 rather than meet a battalion that walked its flanks, and attacked a Regional Force convoy instead; about a third fewer battalions were broken in 1966–67, and no metric showed it. But the reform stopped where the American lever stopped. The list for generals became advisory in 1970, the palace purged the colonels who asked for it back, and Quang Tri in 1972 and the Highlands in 1975 were lost by generals no board had chosen. The army's best staff plan became Thieu's warrant for the retreat of March 1975. Saigon falls on 30 April 1975, at rung (a).

## Memo 008 — A South Vietnamese industrial base one generation above 1964, standing from 1 January 1964: metallurgy and machining; electronics manufacturing

Memorandum 008 gave the Republic, from 1964, the steelworks, arsenal, radio plant and battery works of a country a generation ahead of it, and made its army buy from them from 1965. For ten years the effect was slow and mostly invisible: radios at every post of the held belt, attacked a third less often and answered, after the Front began ambushing the relief at Cai Lay in 1967, by guns instead of trucks; bridges back in weeks; and a rebuild loop that absorbed Vietnamization's equipment. In 1974 it was the first provision to reach the Republic's sustainment after the Americans left: the last aid dollar bought about a third more, the squad guns were fed and the radios stayed on the air. It changed what the vote bought and not the vote, and it reached none of the decisions of March 1975. Tested against the critical path, it delayed the collapse by days, not the three weeks that would have mattered. The 4th Corps took the plants intact. Saigon falls on 30 April 1975, at rung (a).

## Memo 009 — Basic training to the 2026 standard for every US and RVNAF enlisted entrant from 1957, with an abridged course for the Regional and Popular Forces

Memorandum 009 trained every private soldier of both armies from 1957, the Americans to their services' 2026 courses, the ARVN to a ten-week course on the same programme and the territorials to six weeks of it, and found that training changes who lives, not who wins. Every soldier carried the tourniquet drill, and about 5,000–14,000 men lived who had died historically, at Thuan Loi, at Albany and in the streets at Tet. The trained post held its first ten minutes nineteen times in twenty; the trained battalion was attacked less, so its gain was invisible. The enemy answered by moving his war to the mine in Quang Nam, to the sapper, and to the self-defence hamlets of 1968, and the devaluation of 1966 sent trained deserters home and some to the Front's guerrillas. The mobilization of 1968 was a month later and trained. Nothing reached the generals, the soldier's family or the aid vote. Saigon falls on 30 April 1975, at rung (a).

## Memo 010 — NCO education to the 2026 US standard for every US NCO and every RVNAF regular and territorial NCO from 1957, each course a gate for the next promotion

Memorandum 010 schooled every sergeant of both armies for his grade from 1957, the Americans in their services' 2026 courses and the ARVN and its territorials at the academy at Dong De, each course a gate for the next stripe. It completed what 007 and 009 began: from 1964 the Republic's squads and platoons were led by men taught the job, and when the field commissions emptied a squad, a corporal who had passed the leader's course took it. At Hau My in November 1966 a company that lost its officers in two minutes held, and lost fourteen men instead of forty to sixty; in the mobilization of 1968 one new PF platoon in fifteen lacked a schooled leader, not one in three. The enemy declined what kept its routine, read the routine from the academy's own manuals, and took what did not keep it. The gate survived the palace's decree of 1970, the only merit rule that did. None of it reached the corps commanders or the soldiers' families. Saigon falls on 30 April 1975, at rung (a).

## Settled positions

- **POSTNA-1** · vars: GVN.political_stability, POP.gvn_legitimacy, POP.land_tenure · The binding deficit on the opening date is political: no provision that leaves the Saigon government's standing in the countryside unchanged moves the end state above rung (b), whatever it does to the enemy's forces (TNA G-1)
- **POSTNA-2** · vars: POP.night_control, RFPF.effectiveness · Night control of a hamlet is held only by security resident in it with a means of calling help and a reaction that arrives in the dark; mobile forces that leave at dusk do not change it (TNA G-2)
- **POSTNA-3** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, ENEMY.regeneration, SANCT.laos, SANCT.cambodia · While the enemy controls whether to accept battle and regenerates in sanctuary, attrition has no crossover point; a strategy that waits for one waits for something the geometry does not permit (TNA G-8)
- **POSTNA-4** · vars: TRAIL.capacity, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving · On the opening date the enemy's external requirement from the North is of the order of 20 tons a day against a Trail of 20–30 tons a day and an uncounted sea route; Trail capacity is elastic with labour, so interdiction is judged only by tonnage arriving below the requirement, never by trucks or porters destroyed (TNA G-9)
- **POSTNA-5** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.credibility_gap, US.casualties · The American political clock is spent by casualties, cost and time, and fastest by the discovery that reported progress was false; a provision that improves a metric without improving the war shortens the clock (TNA G-5, G-10)
- **POSTNA-6** · vars: ADVISE.leverage, POP.gvn_legitimacy · Advisory leverage trades short-run effectiveness against long-run legitimacy; no position on that line is free, and every proposal to increase leverage states what it costs the Republic's claim to be its own government (TNA G-6)
- **POS001-1** · vars: POP.land_tenure, POP.gvn_legitimacy, POP.night_control · Land reform changes what the government's arrival means, not whether it arrives: its value in any hamlet equals the night security behind it, and titles issued are never evidence of allegiance (001 §2 F001-4, F001-10; §4.P2)
- **POS001-2** · vars: GVN.corruption, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.political_stability · An independent anti-corruption body in the Republic survives only with a Vietnamese patron and an American lever; its durable effect is on muster, pay and documentary cases below the top, and its reach upward ends when the lever lapses with the American drawdown (001 §4.P4)
- **POS001-3** · vars: HANOI.will · Reform that erodes the Front's base raises Hanoi's urgency and shifts the arguments inside the Politburo; it does not change Hanoi's commitment to armed reunification or the timing of its decisions to invade (001 §2 F001-12; §4.P2)
- **POS001-4** · vars: POP.gvn_legitimacy, VCI.strength · A one-band gain in the countryside's allegiance does not carry into the conventional battles of 1972 and 1975; the end state turns on the military balance after the American withdrawal, and political gains are necessary but not sufficient to move it (001 §4.N)
- **POS002-1** · vars: GVN.police, FIND.vci, POP.night_control · A rural police and Special Branch attack the infrastructure, not the main force; their value in any village equals the night security beside them, and where they work best their arrest count falls, so arrest counts and quotas are never the measure of them (002 F002-11, F002-17; §4.P2)
- **POS002-2** · vars: GVN.admin_capacity, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.political_stability · Merit selection of province and district chiefs survives the coups only with the American aid lever behind it; when the lever lapses with the drawdown the President captures the Board without abolishing it, and its durable gain is the chiefs' experience below the palace (002 §4.P4, EV002-6)
- **POS002-3** · vars: GVN.police, GVN.political_stability, POP.gvn_legitimacy · A stronger and better-recorded police in a coup-prone state is used by the government of the day against its domestic opposition, and its records are a list of loyalties the enemy can capture; both costs are paid and do not outweigh the gain in the held belt (002 F002-9, F002-16; §4.P2, §4.P3)
- **POS003-1** · vars: FIND.main_force, FIX.capability, STRIKE.responsiveness · Airborne radar and signals reconnaissance find the enemy's movement in the open and his headquarters' transmitters, never his regiments under canopy; their value in any engagement equals what can be put on a track within the hour, and an improvement in finding is never claimed as an improvement in fixing (003 §2 F003-5; §4.P2–P5)
- **POS003-2** · vars: INFIL.sea, SANCT.cambodia, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving · In this war the sea route to the South's coast closed in 1964 under observation and the enemy's southern supply moved to Sihanoukville from June 1965; supply through Cambodia, not by sea, is the principal external line into III and IV Corps from 1965 until Lon Nol's coup (003 §2 F003-3; EV003-2)
- **POS003-3** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.credibility_gap · In this war no attack of 4 August 1964 was claimed and Pierce Arrow was not flown; the Southeast Asia Resolution rests on the attack of 2 August, and the Tonkin deception is not part of the credibility gap in any later phase (003 §4.P1, §4.P3; EV000-3)
- **POS004-1** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, ENEMY.engagement_control · Infantry small arms change how the fights the enemy accepts go, never which fights he accepts; at the outpost their value equals the platoon's presence after dark and the reaction behind it, and the enemy's answer to a better-armed post is to attack what is not rearmed (004 F004-1, F004-3, F004-16; §4.P1)
- **POS004-2** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance · In this war the ARVN and the RF/PF carry modern carbines from 1964, and the 1967 M16 crisis and inquiry and the 1968–69 rearmament do not occur; from 1969 the historical army has caught up, and the remaining difference is the squad gun, the marksman and the practice (004 F004-6; §4.P2–P4)
- **POS004-3** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, LOG.distribution · Abundant American ammunition from 1964 deepens the RVNAF's dependence on volume of fire; the 1974 ration falls hardest on the squad gun, and the divisional hoards built against it are lost in the collapse of March 1975 (004 F004-15; §4.P6)
- **POS005-1** · vars: STRIKE.responsiveness, FIND.main_force, FIX.capability · GPS weapons change what dies at a measured coordinate, never what can be located; in this war the J's precision is decisive where the enemy holds still long enough to be measured, at the siege and the fixed crossing, and adds nothing against the main force under canopy or the infrastructure in the hamlets (005 §2 F005-1, F005-7, F005-21)
- **POS005-2** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, FIX.capability, US.political_tolerance · In this war the defence of besieged positions from 1965 rests on the B-52J and an American coordinate cell; it is far stronger while American air power is present and leaves the RVNAF more dependent on it when it goes (005 §2 F005-20)
- **POS005-3** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, FIX.capability · In this war from Khe Sanh onward the PAVN does not lay a set-piece siege to a position the Americans can measure, until the conventional offensive of 1972 forces it to besiege An Loc and Kontum; it loses that one way of choosing its battles while the B-52J and the coordinate cell are present, and regains it when they leave in 1973 (005 §4.P3, §4.P5; EV000-41, EV000-76, EV000-77)
- **POS005-4** · vars: TRAIL.capacity, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving · In this war the panhandle's fixed crossings were cut by the B-52J from April 1966, and Group 559 rebuilt the net as braided fords, causeways and pontoons with no single point of failure; from 1966 the Trail is more redundant than history's, and precision strikes on crossings are never counted as reductions in tonnage arriving (005 §4.P2; EV005-2, EV000-55)
- **POSCP01-1** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.credibility_gap · The small gains on the American clock in memoranda 001–005 (no Tonkin deception, honest damage assessment, no M16 scandal, a conviction in 1967, fewer prisoners and no Bach Mai in 1972) narrow the credibility gap and do not move tolerance by a band in any phase, because the clock was spent by the casualties of 1965–68 and by Tet, which no provision changed and one made sharper (CP01 §3; C003-3)
- **POSCP01-2** · vars: ADVISE.leverage, ARVN.self_sufficiency · In this war the American lever was used to protect the Republic's honest institutions from its own governments and never to make the Republic own the instruments of the conventional war (coordinates, reconnaissance, guided weapons, ammunition stocks); the dependence deepened by memoranda 004 and 005 was never contested by the instrument that could have contested it (CP01 §3)
- **POSCP01-3** · vars: ARVN.leadership, GVN.admin_capacity · The Commission, the Selection Board and every provision that needs a competent leader draw on one pool of perhaps 900–1,200 honest, able field-grade officers in 1964–66; the pool is spent several times over and the divisions are the loser each time, which is why G-4 stays open while the provinces improve (CP01 §3)
- **POS006-1** · vars: FIND.vci, VCI.strength, POP.night_control · Phung Hoang adds the layer above the hamlet to what the Special Branch knows, only where the night is held; outside the held belt it is the historical Phoenix whatever its rules, and its audited count, which falls where it works best, is the measure, never its arrest count (006 F006-15, F006-18, F006-26)
- **POS006-2** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, ENEMY.engagement_control · Unit rotation makes the American battalion fight better in the contacts it gets and changes neither which contacts it gets nor the late-war breakdown of discipline; it gives the enemy a relief window to aim at, and it does not prevent atrocity (006 F006-6, F006-16, F006-19)
- **POS006-3** · vars: ADVISE.leverage, ARVN.self_sufficiency · The selected advisory corps deepens influence, not authority; its durable values are continuity across the American unit's relief and honest reporting, and a better adviser deepens the advised unit's dependence on American fire unless he hands over the radio, which works for artillery, the VNAF and medevac and not for the B-52J (006 F006-2, F006-17, F006-23)
- **POS006-4** · vars: FIND.vci, INTEL.penetration, GVN.political_stability · In this war the national Phung Hoang file, built to warrant standard from 1964, was moved into the Central Intelligence Organization in 1970, consolidated in one building for the 1971 election, and captured intact on 30 April 1975 with the I Corps files a month earlier; the accuracy that made it valuable to the Republic made it more valuable to the victors (006 §4.P4, §4.P6; EV002-6, EV000-94, EV000-98)

- **POS006-6** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, US.personnel_demand · In this war American battalions deploy, are relieved and withdraw as units; the estimated saving of 1,000–2,000 American lives in 1966–69 is a judgment on a rate of 3–6 percent shown so far only at Dien Ban, and does not move the casualty band (006 §4.P2, §4.H; EV006-3)
- **POS007-1** · vars: ARVN.leadership, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war the ARVN's battalions from 1965–67 are commanded by officers a board chose on written criteria and two raters' reports, for eighteen months, with relief for cause; this puts ARVN effectiveness at the cap of the bands in 1966–68, and the enemy answers by declining the better battalion and attacking the unreformed unit beside it, so the gain appears as battalions not lost rather than in any metric (007 §4.P2; EV007-2, EV007-3)
- **POS007-2** · vars: ARVN.leadership, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.political_stability · The ranked list for generals and division commands works only while the American aid condition protects it; in this war it filled one or two division commands in ten against the palace's preference by 1967, became advisory on 12 January 1970, and never governed the corps, so that the decisive commands of 1972 and 1975 were chosen as they were historically (007 §4.P4, §4.P5; EV007-4, EV007-5)

- **POS008-4** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, STRIKE.responsiveness · From 1967 the territorial post's first call is for fire, not men, after the Front's ambush of the relief at My Phuoc Tay; this makes the post cheaper to hold and keeps the platoon behind its wire, so that the post is held better and the hamlet outside it is not, and the call passes to Vietnamese district guns in 1970–71 (008 §4.P2, §4.P4; EV008-4, EV008-7)
- **POS008-5** · vars: GVN.corruption, ADVISE.leverage, ARVN.self_sufficiency · The Directorate of Defence Industry fell to the palace in February 1970 with the four other institutions built behind the American lever; its output and the domestic share survived because the Joint General Staff wanted them, and honest lot acceptance did not, costing perhaps a tenth to a fifth of the base's 1974 value (008 §4.P4; EV002-6)
- **POS009-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · Basic training changes how the fights the enemy accepts go and how many wounded live after them, never which fights he accepts; in this war the ARVN of 1964–65 stands a band above history on the course, the carbine and the educated lieutenant together, and the enemy answers the trained soldier with the mine, the sapper and the untrained target (009 §4.P1, §4.P2; EV002-2, EV009-2, EV009-4)
- **POS009-2** · vars: MED.survival, US.casualties, US.political_tolerance · In this war every soldier of both armies is taught the tourniquet in basic training; the saving is a judgment on a rate of two to four percent of killed in action, shown at Albany and in the first wave of Tet, about 900–1,900 Americans and 4,000–12,000 South Vietnamese, below a band on every variable and proof against enemy adaptation (009 §4.P2, §4.P3, §4.N; EV000-23, EV000-42)
- **POS009-3** · vars: ARVN.desertion, ECON.inflation, VCI.strength · Training does not reach desertion, which follows the soldier's pay, rice and family; the trained deserter carries the course home, and a few hundred a year in the Saigon belt carry it to the Front's guerrillas (009 §4.P2; EV009-3)
- **POS010-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war every RVNAF and territorial NCO since 1957 has passed the course for his grade, and empty squads are given to corporals first class who passed the leader's course; this changes how squads and posts fight the fights the enemy accepts, never which fights he accepts, and the enemy answers by passing the units that keep the routine and attacking those that do not, so the gain appears as companies not destroyed and posts not attacked (010 F010-19, F010-25; EV010-3, EV010-4)
- **POS010-2** · vars: ARVN.leadership, ADVISE.leverage, GVN.political_stability · The NCO promotion gate is a Vietnamese rule enforced by the training command and the boards below colonel; it was broken by the National Day decree of 1 November 1970 and repaired within a year by barring the next promotion, and it is the one merit rule of 1964 that survived the lapse of the American lever, because it threatened no one the palace cared about (010 EV010-6, F010-5)
- **POS010-3** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, US.personnel_demand · American NCO education from 1957 makes the American squad better in the patrol base and the night ambush and saves about 300–900 American lives, a judgment on a rate of one to three percent of small-unit deaths, below a band; it costs the senior NCOs of 1966–67 and does not prevent the decay of 1969–71 (010 F010-12, F010-18, F010-22; EV010-2, EV010-5)
- **POS010-4** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, STRIKE.responsiveness · The American NCO course carries the habit of fixing the enemy and calling fire down to the ARVN squad; it is a strength the Republic owns only where the gun at the other end is Vietnamese, as at Long My, and a dependence everywhere else (010 F010-24; EV008-7)

## Standing directives

- **DIRCP01-1** · In each Part 3, take at least one causal chain from an earlier memorandum whose later links fall in a phase this memorandum revises, and test it against the war as now written; where the new provision or free play makes it resolve differently, say so in the chain review and let it (every chain in memoranda 001–005 resolved as predicted, which is more likely tidiness than foresight)
- **DIRCP01-2** · A war-wide figure for lives saved, or any war-wide count built from a rate, must be shown at work in at least two dated events in the chapters before a later memorandum repeats it; until then it is cited as a judgment resting on its rate, with the rate named (CP01 calibration of the [X-004] lives-saved figure)
- **DIRMT01-1** · In every §4.N, state the date of the Republic's fall as its own estimate, separately from the rung: a window, the mechanisms in the cumulative force that pull it earlier and those that pull it later, and which dominate and why; "on the historical timeline" may be written only as the conclusion of that test, and a change of date is reported as a change of date and does not by itself move the rung between (a) and (b) while the ladder's overlap stands (the historical fall, twenty-five months after the last American combat troops left, satisfies the words of rung (b), and seven memoranda have kept (a) and (b) apart by the date alone)
- **DIRMT01-2** · In every §4.N, carry a running sum of the sub-band estimates that all memoranda so far have made on the same variable (American dead, ARVN battalions not lost, and the like), tagged as exercise judgments with their rates named, and say whether the sum crosses a band; and treat the American aid appropriation of 1974 and the refusal of April 1975 as events a provision can change, not as history to be carried (each memorandum judged its own saving of American lives alone, and the 1974 vote was never examined)
- **DIRMT01-3** · Where a chapter's end vector returns a variable to the historical state from a non-zero band in the phase before, the chapter must contain the dated events that produce the convergence; and in every memorandum that revises Phase VI, state in the phase's analysis the Republic's state at the end of 1974, before the last offensive, because the phase's end vector is measured after the fall and cannot record anything the fall erased (Phase V returned four countryside variables to history with no sentence on the countryside, and Phase VI's vector is blind by construction)
- **DIRMT01-4** · Where a memorandum alters an event and keeps its historical outcome, name what absorbs the difference (the enemy's choice to bypass or decline, a decision above the level the provision reached, an external fixed by law or by another government) and show it in the event; "as historically" is a conclusion, never a mechanism (in Phase VI at least six altered events in the last campaign restore the historical outcome by statement)
- **DIRMT01-5** · Where a perverse effect or a capture undoes a gain, state the net in both directions with its weight, and where several provisions' institutions fall to the same mechanism in the same years, judge them together before judging each alone (four institutions from four memoranda fall to the lapse of the American lever in 1970–71, each judged alone, and every memorandum closes on the gain undone)
- **DIRMT01-6** · The next memorandum or review whose Part 3 revises Phase V or VI states the PAVN's 1972 losses in this war against the historical figure and the rebuilding time that follows, before writing 1973–75 (memorandum 005 made the measured sieges the enemy's worst battles; Phase V keeps the historical losses and Phase VI the historical rebuilding)
- **DIRMT01-7** · Every memorandum whose Part 3 revises Phase V or VI tests its effects against the critical path of 1975 (the palace's orders of 13–14 March, the 1st Corps' march against the rains, and Minh's surrender) and states whether any mechanism could delay the collapse of I and II Corps by about three weeks, the threshold beyond which the assault falls into the rains; effects on fights the PAVN could bypass are reported as such (the date of the fall was carried for seven memoranda without its critical path ever being stated)
- **DIRMT01-8** · Every memorandum touching the countryside states its effect separately for the Delta, the coastal lowlands of I and II Corps, the Highlands and their peoples, and the Saigon belt, and names a place in each where the effect is shown or says why there is none (the Delta was written as a footnote, the Montagnards appear twice and FULRO never, and Binh Dinh vanished from the record after 1967)
- **DIRMT01-9** · Every provision touching the reliability of the ARVN or the territorial forces addresses the soldier's family: where it lives, what his pay buys after inflation, and what happens to it when the unit moves or the front gives way (the corps of 1975 dissolved toward their families, and no memorandum had treated them)
- **DIRMT01-10** · The enemy's decisions have authors: in each memorandum name the body or commander who took the enemy's decision of G3, and distinguish Hanoi, the B-2 Front and COSVN, and the regional fronts where they differed; treat the Soviet and Chinese supply as variables with their own politics (COSVN vanishes from the record after 1971, the Phuoc Long argument is told as one mind, and the Soviet deliveries of 1974 are absent)
- **DIRMT01-11** · Every memorandum touching the countryside or the RVNAF states its effect on rice (production, procurement and the Front's take) and on the piaster and the soldier's pay, with at least one dated event (rice appears eleven times in Phase II and once in 1972–75, the years the economy decided)

## Gap register (latest status)

- **G-1** · A state without a foundation · narrowed · Land, police, merit chiefs and the Commission give the Republic a government in the held belt from 1964; it is captured by the palace when the American lever lapses in 1970–71, and its foundation in the countryside does not carry into the conventional war (CP01)
- **G-2** · Who holds the countryside after dark · narrowed · Posts with their platoon and a reaction hold about nine attacks in ten, and the held belt is held at night before Tet; outside it nothing has changed, and every programme stops at its edge (CP01)
- **G-3** · Identifying the infrastructure inside the population · narrowed · A Special Branch, a census and a land register identify the infrastructure in the held belt from 1964 and drive it out; it moves to the towns, penetrates the Branch, and turns the census into the Hue lists (CP01)
- **G-4** · The officer corps: selection, leadership, desertion, corruption · narrowed · Battalions and regiments are commanded from 1965–66 by board-chosen officers educated since 1957, and the enemy declines them; the divisions and corps stay the palace's choices, and the decisive commands of 1972 and 1975 are chosen as historically (MT01)
- **G-5** · The American political clock · open · The provisions saved perhaps 2,500–5,000 American lives, below a band; tolerance unmoved in every phase, and the 1974 appropriation now examined and unmoved (MT01)
- **G-6** · Advisory leverage and its limits · open · The Aid Compliance Board is a real lever until 1969 and lapses with the withdrawal; it was used for governance and never for the RVNAF's self-sufficiency (CP01)
- **G-7** · Finding and fixing the main force · open · The enemy is easier to see in the open and exactly as hard to find under canopy; he still chooses every fight except the siege (CP01)
- **G-8** · Sanctuary and the theory of attrition · open · Cambodia is counted from 1965 and its caches fall in ten days in 1970; the sanctuaries still regenerate the main force in every phase (CP01)
- **G-9** · The Trail: throughput required against capacity · open · Measured from 1965 instead of guessed; bombing taxes it by about a tenth at best, and the B-52J built it a net with no single point of failure (CP01)
- **G-10** · The measurement problem · narrowed · The radar's ledger, the musters and the Phoenix audit give honest counts of the Trail, the army and the infrastructure; body count and the Hamlet Evaluation System remain as corrupt as before (CP01)
- **G-11** · The sea and Sihanoukville · narrowed · The sea route closed in 1964; Sihanoukville opened eighteen months early and was counted, not stopped, until Lon Nol closed it in 1970 (CP01)
- **G-12** · Air power against a dispersed, night-moving enemy · narrowed · Decisive against the measured siege and the fixed crossing; nothing against a regiment under canopy or an attack on a post at night, and none of it Vietnamese (CP01)
- **G-13** · No single manager of the war · open · CORDS on its historical date and form; the provisions created no single manager, only better inheritances for it (CP01)
- **G-14** · No lever on Hanoi's will · open · Nothing in the force reaches the Politburo; the timing of its last campaign was its own, set by the 1st Corps' road and the rains, and only a three-week delay in the collapse of I and II Corps would have moved it (MT01)
- **G-15** · The theater base · open · Unchanged by any provision; the rearmament's ammunition and the J's kits ride the historical base (CP01)
- **G-16** · Personnel spaces · narrowed · Unit rotation and a selected eighteen-month advisory corps since 1964 change how soldiers are rotated and advisers chosen; spaces remain trivial against a ceiling of none, and nothing a provision has built survives the withdrawal of 1973 (MT01)
- **G-17** · The soldier's family · open · ARVN soldiers' families lived beside their units on pay that could not keep them; in March 1975 the corps dissolved toward them, and no provision has addressed dependants' housing, pay against inflation or the movement of families (MT01)

## The enemy's war — Hanoi's decisions in sequence

### The enemy's decisions

### The first posts and the Front's answer
*1 Mar 1964 – 31 Jul 1965 · The Delta along the Bassac and the Mekong, the provinces around Saigon, and the coastal Centre from Quang Nam to Binh Dinh · P1 · new · EV002-2*

The first village police post was settled at Phu Tan in An Giang on 1 March 1964, in the Hoa Hao country where the titling teams would begin six weeks later, and the posts thereafter followed the titling line into villages the government held at night (EC002-1) [X-002]. Each was a brick house with a radio, an AN/PRC-10 or one of the HT-1 village sets, ten constables armed with M1 carbines and a Thompson or a BAR, and, by the programme's rule, a Popular Forces platoon in the same village [X-002].

### The Can Giuoc killings
*9 Jun – 14 Jul 1964 · Can Giuoc and Can Duoc Districts, Long An Province · P1 · new · EV001-3*

In May 1964 titling teams from Tan An began work in the villages of Can Giuoc and Can Duoc, the rice districts of Long An between Saigon and the sea, where the survey of December 1963 had found most of the strategic hamlets destroyed and the Front's infrastructure intact [H] [X-001]. The province chief, under pressure from Saigon for a showcase close to the capital, sent the teams into hamlets the government held by day only and posted the claimants' names in the village offices, as the procedure then required (EC001-4) [X-001].

### The camps, the bases and the towns: Nam Dong, Bien Hoa and Song Be
*6 Jul 1964 – 12 May 1965 · Nam Dong CIDG camp west of Da Nang; Bien Hoa air base; Song Be and Phuoc Binh, Phuoc Long Province · P1 · changed from history · EVCP01-3*

Three attacks are told together because they showed one thing three ways: the enemy chose the night and the target, and what held was whatever was already inside the wire. At 02:30 on 6 July 1964 about two battalions of VC and PAVN, some 800–900 men, attacked the CIDG camp at Nam Dong near the Laotian border, held by Special Forces Detachment A-726 under Captain Roger H.

### The Gulf of Tonkin incidents and the Southeast Asia Resolution
*2–11 Aug 1964 · Gulf of Tonkin and Washington · P1 · changed from history · EV000-3*

On 30–31 July 1964 South Vietnamese commando boats under the covert OPLAN 34A programme, run by MACV's Studies and Observations Group, raided the North Vietnamese islands of Hon Me and Hon Ngu [H7]. On 2 August the destroyer USS *Maddox*, on a DESOTO signals intelligence patrol under Captain John J.

### Hanoi commits the regulars; the Trail and the first air war in Laos
*Sep 1964 – Apr 1965 · North Vietnam, the Laotian panhandle and the Central Highlands · P1 · changed from history · EV000-6*

The Ninth Plenum of the Lao Dong Party Central Committee, in December 1963, had resolved to seek a decisive military victory in the South before the United States could intervene in strength [H]. Through 1964 the Politburo under Le Duan acted on it.

### The trawlers turn back; the Sihanoukville route opens
*Sep 1964 – Jun 1965 · Haiphong and the Gulf of Tonkin; the II Corps coast; Phnom Penh and Sihanoukville (Kompong Som), Cambodia · P1 · new · EV003-2*

Hanoi did not give up the sea at once. After TIDE TABLE's first half-year Group 125 paused through the summer of 1964, and in September, while the Global Hawk orbit was still held in the Gulf of Tonkin after the August crisis, it sent two trawlers south [X-003].

### Saigon's governments and the war in the city
*19 Dec 1964 – 19 Jun 1965 · Saigon · P1 · changed from history · EVCP01-1*

Six months of Saigon's politics are told here as one event, because they were one process: the generals unmaking every government they made, while the Front's city teams showed they could strike anywhere in the capital. In the week before Christmas 1964 the Young Turks, with Khanh's acquiescence, dissolved the High National Council and arrested several of its members; Taylor dressed the officers down, Khanh attacked him publicly, and the Mission's relations with the junta reached their lowest point [H10].

### The battle of Binh Gia
*28 Dec 1964 – 1 Jan 1965 · Binh Gia, Phuoc Tuy Province · P1 · changed from history · EV000-9*

Binh Gia, a Catholic village of northern refugees in Phuoc Tuy Province east of Saigon, was the site of the Viet Cong's first large set-piece battle [H1]. The attackers were the 271st and 272nd Regiments (then called the 1st and 2nd), the nucleus of the forming 9th Division, with the 80th Artillery Detachment and local battalions of the B-2 Front, an estimated 1,800 men [H1].

### The American escalation: Flaming Dart, Rolling Thunder, the Marines and the July decision
*7 Feb – 28 Jul 1965 · Pleiku and Qui Nhon; North Vietnam; Da Nang; Washington · P1 · changed from history · EVCP01-2*

The six months in which the United States went from an advisory war to a war of its own are told here as one event, because each step made the next one. At 01:50 on 7 February 1965, while McGeorge Bundy was in Saigon and Kosygin in Hanoi, about 300 men of the 30th Company of the VC 409th Sapper Battalion attacked Camp Holloway and the advisers' compound at Pleiku, killing seven Americans and wounding 104 and destroying 10 aircraft [H5].

### The battle of Ba Gia
*28–31 May 1965 · Ba Gia, Son Tinh District, Quang Ngai Province · P1 · changed from history · EV000-17*

On 29 May 1965 the VC 1st Regiment of the forming 2nd Division (40th, 60th and 90th Battalions, with the 45th Independent Battalion and local force battalions), directed by PAVN Major General Chu Huy Man, overran the outpost at Loc Tho near Ba Gia, about 10 km from Quang Ngai, and ambushed the ARVN 1st Battalion, 51st Infantry Regiment as it came to help [H11]. On the historical course the battalion was destroyed.

### The battle of Dong Xoai
*9–13 Jun 1965 · Dong Xoai district town and CIDG camp, Phuoc Long Province · P1 · changed from history · EV000-18*

Late on 9 June 1965 the VC 272nd Regiment, with a battalion of the 273rd, a 75mm recoilless rifle company, an 82mm mortar company, a flamethrower company and anti-aircraft machine guns, attacked the district headquarters and CIDG camp at Dong Xoai; the 271st Regiment lay in reserve in the Thuan Loi rubber plantation [H6]. The camp was held by Special Forces Detachment A-342, nine men of Navy Seabee Team 1104, three CIDG companies, the 111th Regional Force Company and militia, with six armoured cars and two 105mm howitzers [H6].

### The big-unit war: Starlite, A Shau, Hastings, Long Tan, Attleboro, Cedar Falls and Junction City
*18 Aug 1965 – 14 May 1967 · The Van Tuong peninsula and the DMZ in I Corps; the A Shau valley; Phuoc Tuy; War Zone C and the Iron Triangle in III Corps · P2 · changed from history · EVCP01-4*

The big-unit battles of 1965–67 are told here together, because together they are the shape of the phase: each won on the ground, each followed by the enemy's return, none changing the war. On 18–24 August 1965, on a deserter's information, the 7th Marines under Colonel Oscar F.

### The Da Nhim line
*3 Oct 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · The 230 kV line from the Da Nhim station at Don Duong, Tuyen Duc Province, through Di Linh in Lam Dong and Long Khanh to the Thu Duc and Bien Hoa substations · P2 · new · EV008-3*

The steelworks ran on electricity it did not make, and the Front found that out in its second year. The melt shop drew 70–100 MW at peak, about half from the line that brought the Da Nhim hydro station's power 250 kilometres down from the Lang Biang plateau to Thu Duc and the rest from the 66 MW thermal station at Thu Duc [M008].

### Plei Me and the Ia Drang
*19 Oct – 18 Nov 1965 · Plei Me CIDG camp and the Ia Drang valley below the Chu Pong massif, Pleiku Province · P2 · changed from history · EV000-23*

On 19 October 1965 the PAVN B3 Front under Major General Chu Huy Man attacked the Special Forces camp at Plei Me, south of Pleiku, and the next day ambushed the ARVN relief column; the relief reached the camp at dusk on 25 October and the PAVN withdrew west towards the Chu Pong massif on the Cambodian border [H27]. The 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile), newly arrived, was turned loose in pursuit.

### The mines of Dien Ban
*1 Mar 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · Dien Ban, Dai Loc and Duy Xuyen Districts, Quang Nam Province, south of Da Nang between Route 1 and the Song Thu Bon; Son Tinh and Binh Son Districts, Quang Ngai Province · P2 · new · EV009-2*

The enemy's answer to the trained soldier was not to fight him; it was to kill him without fighting, and nowhere did that answer cost more than in the hamlets south of Da Nang. In late 1965 the command of the Quang Da Special Zone, under the Military Region 5 Party Committee, reviewed a year of contacts with ARVN battalions and American Marines in Dien Ban and Dai Loc, and concluded that its local-force companies were losing more than they gained in firefights with units that returned aimed fire in the first seconds and did not bunch up when they were hit (F009-20) [X-009].

### Operation OPEN ROAD
*3–21 May 1966 · Route 13 from Chon Thanh to An Loc, the Xa Cam rubber and the Tau O crossing, Binh Long Province; Bau Bang, Binh Duong Province · P2 · new · EV007-3*

The ambush that was never sprung on Route 13 is the clearest case in this war of what the officer reforms did and why no report showed it. In April 1966 the VC 9th Division ordered its 272nd Regiment, three battalions of about 1,500 men with 82mm mortars, 75mm recoilless rifles and RPD guns, to lay an ambush on Route 13 between Chon Thanh and An Loc for the next ARVN convoy to the Binh Long garrison, on the road where the regiment had broken relief columns in 1965 [X-007].

### The relief at Dien Ban
*8–31 Aug 1966 · Dien Ban and Dai Loc Districts, Quang Nam Province, south of Da Nang between Route 1 and the Song Thu Bon · P2 · new · EV006-3*

The relief at Dien Ban was the first time the enemy attacked an American battalion in the week it changed over, and it showed both halves of what unit rotation had done. The 1st Battalion, 9th Marines had come ashore at Da Nang in July 1965 and had spent a year in the hamlets of Dien Ban south of the airfield, the same companies under the same commander throughout [X-006].

### Operation STEADY HAND
*14–19 Nov 1966 · Cai Be District, Dinh Tuong Province, between Route 4 and the Plain of Reeds; the hamlets of Hau My village · P2 · new · EV010-3*

The rice was the reason for both sides. The Mekong flood of September and October 1966 had drowned much of the Plain of Reeds and the main-season crop in the districts north of Route 4, and the Front's Dinh Tuong provincial committee, its own stocks lost in the water, ordered the 263rd Main Force Battalion in late October to escort its rice levy in the hamlets of Cai Be as the harvest came in [X-010].

### The Mo Duc raid and the Phoenix story
*11 Feb – 30 Jun 1967 · Duc Thanh village, Mo Duc District, Quang Ngai Province; Saigon; Hanoi; Washington · P2 · new · EV006-4*

The raid at Duc Thanh was what the method became where the night was not held, and it reached the American press within a month. By the end of 1966 the held belt had little left for the district centres to find (EV002-5), and the corps commanders and the CORDS planners wanted the same results from the contested provinces of I and II Corps, where the Front still ran most villages after dark [X-006].

### The night of the relief at My Phuoc Tay
*9–10 Mar 1967 · The PF post at Ap My Loi and the canal road to Cai Lay district town, My Phuoc Tay village, Cai Lay District, Dinh Tuong Province · P2 · new · EV008-4*

This is the night the radio's second-order effect became visible, and the night that shows it best (F008-3, F008-6). By 1967 every Popular Forces post in the held belt of Dinh Tuong had a set on the district net, a PRC-25 from the Go Vap plant since the previous autumn, and a fresh battery every Thursday from the exchange at the district (EC008-7, EC008-8) [X-008].

### Operation Buffalo and the siege of Con Thien
*2 Jul – 31 Oct 1967 · Con Thien and "the Marketplace", Quang Tri Province, south of the DMZ · P2 · changed from history · EV000-36*

Con Thien, a low hill 2 miles south of the DMZ and the western anchor of the planned strongpoint barrier, was the most exposed Marine position in the country, within range of PAVN artillery north of the Ben Hai [H42]. On 2 July 1967, at a place the Marines called the Marketplace, PAVN forces ambushed and nearly destroyed Company B, 1st Battalion, 9th Marines; it was the single worst day for the Marines in Vietnam, with 86 killed [H42].

### The siege of Khe Sanh
*21 Jan – 15 Apr 1968 · Khe Sanh Combat Base, Lang Vei and the surrounding hills, Quang Tri Province; Route 9 in Laos to Ban Houei Sane · P3 · changed from history · EV000-41*

In January 1968 the PAVN massed around the Marine base at Khe Sanh, in the northwest corner of Quang Tri Province astride Route 9 to Laos. The 304th and 325C Divisions were close in, with the 320th and 324th Divisions in the region [H46].

### The Tet Offensive: the first wave
*30–31 Jan 1968 · Saigon, Hue and the provincial and district capitals of South Vietnam · P3 · changed from history · EV000-42*

Shortly after midnight on 30 January, a day early because of a confusion in calendars, VC and PAVN forces attacked Nha Trang, Ban Me Thuot, Kontum, Hoi An, Tuy Hoa, Da Nang, Qui Nhon and Pleiku in I and II Corps [H39]. The warning was not fully heeded: half the ARVN was on holiday leave for Tet [H].

### The posts of Cai Lay at Tet
*30 Jan – 2 Feb 1968 · Cai Lay and Cai Be Districts, Dinh Tuong Province; the post at Ap My Loi, My Phuoc Tay; the posts along the canal and Route 4 east to My Tho · P3 · new · EV010-4*

The Front's battalions came through Cai Lay to attack My Tho, and most of the posts on the way were left alone. The 514th Local Force Battalion and the 261st and 263rd Main Force Battalions moved east toward the province capital on the nights of 29–31 January, along the canals north of Route 4, and the Dinh Tuong command's order was to isolate the posts on the route rather than take them, because the battalions needed to reach My Tho intact [H] [X-010].

### The battle of Hue
*31 Jan – 2 Mar 1968 · Hue, Thua Thien Province · P3 · changed from history · EV000-44*

In the early hours of 31 January the PAVN 4th, 5th and 6th Regiments with the 1st, 2nd and 12th Sapper Battalions, under a Hue City Front command, took almost all of Hue, the old imperial capital, except the ARVN 1st Division headquarters in the northeast corner of the Citadel and the MACV advisory compound south of the Perfume River [H45]. Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong held his headquarters with his staff and the Hac Bao Reconnaissance Company, and brought in the 3rd Regiment, the 4th Battalion, 2nd Regiment, the 1st Airborne Task Force (2nd and 7th Airborne Battalions), Vietnamese Marin

### The third offensive
*17 Aug – 23 Sep 1968 · Provincial towns and bases, especially in III Corps and the Central Highlands · P3 · changed from history · EV000-52*

The third phase of the general offensive began in mid-August with attacks by fire and ground assaults on towns and bases, including attacks around Tay Ninh in III Corps [H39] [H]. It was weaker than its predecessors: the local forces that had carried the attacks of February and May were largely gone, and the main forces would not commit themselves against American firepower in the same way again [H39].

### The self-defence hamlets
*17 Aug – 31 Oct 1968 · Duc Hue and Trang Bang Districts, Hau Nghia Province; Can Duoc and Rach Kien, Long An Province; Cai Be and Cai Lay Districts, Dinh Tuong Province · P3 · new · EV009-4*

The third offensive went for what the course did not reach, and in the provinces around Saigon that was the People's Self-Defense Force. COSVN's Military Affairs Committee, planning the offensive of August after two waves that had broken on the district towns' walls, ordered its subregions to avoid the RF and PF posts that had held in February and May and to strike the new self-defence groups of the mobilization law, whose members were townsmen and farmers with a Garand and three days' instruction (F009-6) [X-009].

### Commando Hunt and the growth of the Trail
*10 Oct 1970 – Dec 1971 · The Laotian panhandle and northeastern Cambodia · P4 · changed from history · EV000-68*

The dry-season phases of Commando Hunt were the main US effort against the North's logistics after 1968 [H53]. Phase V, from 10 October 1970 to 30 April 1971, claimed 16,266 trucks destroyed, a figure Seventh Air Force itself lowered to 11,000; in Phase VII the AC-130E gunships were credited with 7,335 of 10,689 trucks claimed [H53].

### The Easter Offensive opens: the DMZ front
*30 Mar – 2 Apr 1972 · Quang Tri Province, from the DMZ to the Cua Viet and Camp Carroll · P5 · changed from history · EV000-74*

The armour was seen before it crossed. From 12 March the Gulf watch, standing off the Quang Tri coast outside the SA-2s that the North had moved into and just north of the DMZ, tracked tracked-vehicle columns moving south at night on Route 1A and Route 101 from Vinh Linh toward the Ben Hai, and the panhandle watch tracked others moving east along Route 9 in Laos toward Khe Sanh [X-003].

### The northern districts of Binh Dinh
*Apr – Aug 1972 · Hoai Nhon, Tam Quan and Hoai An districts, Binh Dinh Province · P5 · changed from history · EVMT01-1*

While the world watched Quang Tri, Kontum and An Loc, the PAVN 3rd Division, the Yellow Star, came down out of the An Lao valley in April 1972 and took the three northern districts of Binh Dinh, Hoai Nhon, Tam Quan and Hoai An, from the 22nd Division's 40th and 41st Regiments and the province's Regional Forces; the district towns and the old American base at Landing Zone English were in its hands by the end of the month, and the districts were retaken over the summer [H]. It was the only place in 1972 where the offensive reached a densely peopled coastal lowland and held it for months, and it 

### The Delta during the offensive
*Apr – Oct 1972 · Chuong Thien and Kien Giang provinces; the U Minh forest · P5 · changed from history · EVMT01-2*

When the 21st Division left the Delta in April 1972 to fight its way up Route 13 toward An Loc, the regiments the PAVN and the Front had kept in the U Minh forest came out against the outposts of Chuong Thien and Kien Giang [H]. Historically this is where the offensive reached the Delta's countryside: dozens of posts lost, districts cut off, and the government's figures for its own security falling for the first time since 1968 [H].

### Loc Ninh and the siege of An Loc
*7 Apr – 18 Jun 1972 · Loc Ninh and An Loc, Binh Long Province, on Route 13 · P5 · changed from history · EV000-76*

On 5 April the 5th Division of the PAVN B-2 Front attacked Loc Ninh, on Route 13 near the Cambodian border, and overran it on the afternoon of 7 April; the 9th Division took the Quan Loi base camp that evening, and the 7th Division cut Route 13 south of An Loc at the Tau O bridge with its 141st, 165th and 209th Regiments [H65]. An Loc, the provincial capital 100 km north of Saigon, was cut off by 8 April [H65].

### Tan Canh, Dak To and the battle of Kontum
*24 Apr – 9 Jun 1972 · Tan Canh, Dak To, Ben Het and Kontum city, Kontum Province · P5 · changed from history · EV000-77*

In the Central Highlands the PAVN 320th Division began pressing the firebases on Rocket Ridge in early April, and on 24 April the 2nd Division's 1st and 66th Regiments, with the D10 Sapper Battalion and tanks, overran the ARVN bases at Tan Canh and Dak To II, held by the 42nd and 47th Regiments of the 22nd Division; the division "ceased to exist as a fighting unit", and its commander, Colonel Le Duc Dat, disappeared [H66]. Tan Canh fell in a day, to tanks and infantry already inside the wire before dawn, and nothing in the J reached a fight of that kind (F005-6) [X-005].

### The fall of Quang Tri
*27 Apr – 2 May 1972 · Quang Tri City and Highway 1 south to the My Chanh River · P5 · changed from history · EV000-78*

On 27 April the PAVN renewed its attack on the 3rd Division's defence of Quang Tri City [H]. Contradictory orders from the I Corps commander, Lieutenant General Hoang Xuan Lam, and from Giai left units moving in opposite directions, and on 1 May Giai ordered the city abandoned [H67] [H].

### Resolution 21 and the North's rebuilding
*Oct 1973 – 1974 · Hanoi; the Laotian panhandle and the western Highlands · P6 · changed from history · EV000-87*

In October 1973 the 21st Plenum of the Party Central Committee in Hanoi resolved that the revolution in the South must continue by the path of revolutionary violence, and that the PAVN should respond to Saigon's operations and prepare for a decisive offensive [H]. The PAVN rebuilt through 1973 and 1974: it improved the strategic road along the western side of South Vietnam east of the Truong Son, extended the fuel pipeline into the South, built up stocks of ammunition and armour in the base areas and grouped its divisions into army corps, the 1st Corps in October 1973 and the 4th Corps on 20 J

### The war of attrition of 1974
*16 May – 10 Dec 1974 · The Iron Triangle; Thuong Duc, Duc Duc and Phu Loc in I Corps · P6 · changed from history · EV000-91*

From May 1974 the PAVN took the initiative with a series of "strategic raids" designed to grind down the ARVN and test its reserves [H] [H71]. In III Corps the PAVN 9th Division attacked Rach Bap in the Iron Triangle from 16 May; the ARVN retook it only in November [H71].

### The fall of Phuoc Long
*12 Dec 1974 – 6 Jan 1975 · Phuoc Long Province (Phuoc Binh and Song Be), III Corps · P6 · changed from history · EV000-92*

On 12 December 1974 the PAVN 4th Corps under Hoang Cam, with the 7th Division, the new 3rd Division and independent regiments including the 141st, 165th, 201st and 271st, and two armoured companies with 14 T-54s, attacked Phuoc Long Province on the Cambodian border [H73]. It was defended mainly by Regional Force battalions, reinforced by the 1st and 2nd Battalions, 7th Regiment and the 1st Battalion, 9th Regiment of the 5th Division and the 81st Airborne Ranger Battalion [H73].

### The collapse of I Corps
*13–30 Mar 1975 · Quang Tri, Hue and Da Nang · P6 · changed from history · EV000-94*

On 13 March Thieu ordered Truong to give up most of I Corps and withdrew the Airborne Division towards Saigon as a reserve [H75]. On 20 March he ordered Truong to hold only Da Nang; on 29 March he ordered him to turn back and retake it, which Truong refused [H75].

### The Politburo's calendar: Saigon before the rains
*25 Mar – 14 Apr 1975 · Hanoi and the roads south · P6 · changed from history · EVMT01-4*

The date of the fall of Saigon was set in Hanoi between 25 March and 14 April, and it was set by the rains and by the road. On 25 March, with Hue abandoned and the Highlands column destroyed, the Politburo resolved to take Saigon before the rainy season, which in the southern provinces begins in May and turns the lowlands around the capital to mud; on 31 March, with Da Nang taken, it decided to do it in April; and on 14 April it named the operation the Ho Chi Minh Campaign [H].

### Xuan Loc
*9–21 Apr 1975 · Xuan Loc, Long Khanh Province, northeast of Saigon · P6 · changed from history · EV000-96*

On 9 April the PAVN 4th Corps under Major General Hoang Cam, with the 6th, 7th and 341st Divisions and tanks and artillery, attacked Xuan Loc, the road junction northeast of Saigon on Route 1 [H76]. The town was held by the ARVN 18th Division under Brigadier General Le Minh Dao, with the 1st Airborne Brigade, armoured units, Rangers and Regional Forces, and air support from Bien Hoa and Tan Son Nhut [H76].

### The fall of Saigon
*29–30 Apr 1975 · Saigon · P6 · changed from history · EV000-98*

By late April five PAVN corps, Group 232 and the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th Corps, with 15 infantry divisions and three tank regiments, encircled Saigon in the Ho Chi Minh Campaign [H77]. Rockets and artillery hit Tan Son Nhut on the morning of 29 April; two US Marine guards, Corporal Charles McMahon and Lance Corporal Darwin Judge, were killed, the last American servicemen killed in action in Vietnam [H].

### Settled positions about the enemy

- **POSTNA-3** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, ENEMY.regeneration, SANCT.laos, SANCT.cambodia · While the enemy controls whether to accept battle and regenerates in sanctuary, attrition has no crossover point; a strategy that waits for one waits for something the geometry does not permit (TNA G-8)
- **POS001-3** · vars: HANOI.will · Reform that erodes the Front's base raises Hanoi's urgency and shifts the arguments inside the Politburo; it does not change Hanoi's commitment to armed reunification or the timing of its decisions to invade (001 §2 F001-12; §4.P2)
- **POS001-4** · vars: POP.gvn_legitimacy, VCI.strength · A one-band gain in the countryside's allegiance does not carry into the conventional battles of 1972 and 1975; the end state turns on the military balance after the American withdrawal, and political gains are necessary but not sufficient to move it (001 §4.N)
- **POS004-1** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, ENEMY.engagement_control · Infantry small arms change how the fights the enemy accepts go, never which fights he accepts; at the outpost their value equals the platoon's presence after dark and the reaction behind it, and the enemy's answer to a better-armed post is to attack what is not rearmed (004 F004-1, F004-3, F004-16; §4.P1)
- **POS005-3** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, FIX.capability · In this war from Khe Sanh onward the PAVN does not lay a set-piece siege to a position the Americans can measure, until the conventional offensive of 1972 forces it to besiege An Loc and Kontum; it loses that one way of choosing its battles while the B-52J and the coordinate cell are present, and regains it when they leave in 1973 (005 §4.P3, §4.P5; EV000-41, EV000-76, EV000-77)
- **POS006-1** · vars: FIND.vci, VCI.strength, POP.night_control · Phung Hoang adds the layer above the hamlet to what the Special Branch knows, only where the night is held; outside the held belt it is the historical Phoenix whatever its rules, and its audited count, which falls where it works best, is the measure, never its arrest count (006 F006-15, F006-18, F006-26)
- **POS006-2** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, ENEMY.engagement_control · Unit rotation makes the American battalion fight better in the contacts it gets and changes neither which contacts it gets nor the late-war breakdown of discipline; it gives the enemy a relief window to aim at, and it does not prevent atrocity (006 F006-6, F006-16, F006-19)
- **POS007-1** · vars: ARVN.leadership, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war the ARVN's battalions from 1965–67 are commanded by officers a board chose on written criteria and two raters' reports, for eighteen months, with relief for cause; this puts ARVN effectiveness at the cap of the bands in 1966–68, and the enemy answers by declining the better battalion and attacking the unreformed unit beside it, so the gain appears as battalions not lost rather than in any metric (007 §4.P2; EV007-2, EV007-3)
- **REVMT01-1** · reverses POS001-3 · vars: HANOI.will, ENEMY.engagement_control, PAVN.strength_south · Hanoi's commitment to armed reunification is fixed throughout and nothing in the force reaches it (G-14); the timing of its offensives is not fixed, and the schedule of the last campaign in particular was set week by week by the ARVN's behaviour in 1975 (the plan for 1976 accelerated after Phuoc Long and again after the Highlands, EV000-92); a memorandum that changes the ARVN, the PAVN's losses or the Republic's state on the eve of the offensive must test what it does to that schedule (MT01 M-6, M-10, M-12)
- **POSMT01-2** · vars: PAVN.strength_south, ENEMY.regeneration · In this war the PAVN's killed and wounded in 1972 were about a tenth above the historical figure, concentrated in the 5th, 7th, 9th, 320th and 2nd Divisions at An Loc and Kontum; the North replaced the men within its 1973 flow and formed its corps on the historical dates, so the extra loss cost the 1974–75 divisions quality and not time (MT01 M-1; EV000-87)
- **POSMT01-3** · vars: HANOI.will, PAVN.strength_south, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The date of the Republic's fall, 30 April 1975 within a window of about 27 April to the first days of May, is derived and not carried: it was set by Hanoi's resolution of 25 March to finish before the rains and by the 1st Corps' march, and only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps would have moved it, by putting the assault into the rains; better ARVN units act on fights the PAVN bypasses and do not reach that threshold (MT01 M-12; EVMT01-4, EV000-96)
- **POSMT01-4** · vars: POP.night_control, VCI.strength, POP.gvn_legitimacy, FIND.vci · The countryside at the end of 1972 is not history's: where a PAVN division sat in the peopled lowlands (northern Binh Dinh, Quang Tri) the gains of 1964–71 were lost, while the held belt of the Delta and the Saigon region kept its posts and files and stays one band better at night and against the infrastructure; the government's legitimacy returns to history's through the decrees of 1972 (MT01 M-4; EVMT01-1, EVMT01-2, EVMT01-3)
- **POS008-2** · vars: POP.night_control, RFPF.effectiveness, STRIKE.responsiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · A radio kept on the air at the post supplies the means of calling help in POSTNA-2 and moves the post's binding constraint to the reaction and fire within range; the Front answers by attacking the relief and the posts that cannot call, and the radio's gain appears as attacks not made (008 §2 F008-1, F008-3, F008-6, F008-16)
- **POS008-3** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, US.political_tolerance, HANOI.will · In this war the Republic's own arsenal and battery works stretched the fiscal 1975 appropriation to about $850 million–$1 billion of history's and kept its ammunition and communications from going dark in 1974, but delayed the collapse of I and II Corps by days, not the three weeks that would have moved the date; domestic sustainment without an air arm the Republic owns and a choice of corps commanders does not move the rung (008 §4.P6, §4.N; EV000-89, EVMT01-4)
- **POS009-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · Basic training changes how the fights the enemy accepts go and how many wounded live after them, never which fights he accepts; in this war the ARVN of 1964–65 stands a band above history on the course, the carbine and the educated lieutenant together, and the enemy answers the trained soldier with the mine, the sapper and the untrained target (009 §4.P1, §4.P2; EV002-2, EV009-2, EV009-4)
- **POS009-3** · vars: ARVN.desertion, ECON.inflation, VCI.strength · Training does not reach desertion, which follows the soldier's pay, rice and family; the trained deserter carries the course home, and a few hundred a year in the Saigon belt carry it to the Front's guerrillas (009 §4.P2; EV009-3)
- **POS010-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war every RVNAF and territorial NCO since 1957 has passed the course for his grade, and empty squads are given to corporals first class who passed the leader's course; this changes how squads and posts fight the fights the enemy accepts, never which fights he accepts, and the enemy answers by passing the units that keep the routine and attacking those that do not, so the gain appears as companies not destroyed and posts not attacked (010 F010-19, F010-25; EV010-3, EV010-4)
